speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: I will then outline how the HIB will help Ministry of Health (MOH) achieve the goal of "One Patient, One Health Summary, One Care Journey", and bring Members of the House through the key provisions of the Bill, before finally covering our plans to commence the Bill from early 2027.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This is why we are transforming our healthcare delivery, from being hospital-centric to delivering care in the community.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: We are implementing national programmes like Healthier SG and Age Well SG, as well as initiatives, such as the Home Personal Care and Mobile Inpatient Care @ Home.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Patients will receive care from a wider range of healthcare providers, not just at public hospitals and polyclinics, but also at home or in the community, including at general practitioner (GP) clinics, dialysis centres and via home medical or rehabilitation services.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: The sharing of a patient's key health information across settings and service providers is therefore essential.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Such sharing of health information will also benefit younger patients who visit new healthcare providers or encounter medical emergencies.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Currently, when patients move between healthcare providers, such as from private specialist clinics to their GPs, their key health records are often not accessible across providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Such gaps can risk medication errors, delayed treatment and duplicate tests and procedures.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This is why many jurisdictions, such as Australia, Estonia, Finland and Norway, have developed robust governance frameworks to govern the sharing of health information across healthcare providers.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This sharing regime has led to better patient outcomes, reduced costs and more effective and efficient healthcare delivery.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: We have studied these jurisdictions carefully and adopted key features suited to our local context.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: But, Sir, in practice, we are not starting from scratch.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Today, all public hospitals and polyclinics are already contributing key health information to NEHR.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: And with Healthier SG, most GP clinics are already onboarded to NEHR.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: This has been of tremendous benefit for GPs and their patients.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Most private hospitals have also onboarded to NEHR, while the remaining are in the process of doing so.

speaker: The Senior Minister of State for Health (Mr Tan Kiat How) (for the Coordinating Minister for Social Policies and Minister for Health)
text: Hence, the vast bulk of key healthcare services are already on NEHR, or coming onboard soon, leaving a small group that have not done so, such as specialist clinics, clinical and radiological laboratories and dental clinics.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Members may also access the handout through the MP@SGPARL App.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This will allow patients' key health information to be accessible by their healthcare providers when they move across healthcare settings.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Patients will benefit from better coordinated care, enhanced quality of care and lower costs.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ms Kamala regularly visits her nearby GP to manage her chronic health conditions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: When she visits a different GP near her new home, the doctor there can make informed care decisions based on Ms Kamala's health information in NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Her new doctor can see which tests have been done and the medications that have been prescribed.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: He need not repeat the tests, saving Ms Kamala time and money.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Appropriate tests and medications can also be ordered to better manage Ms Kamala's health requirements.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Patients moving between private and public healthcare providers, or acute and community settings will similarly benefit.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Actually, I think many Members in the House can relate to these examples.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We often see our residents, especially our seniors, sitting in front of a GP clinic, carrying a big plastic bag of medicine.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I once joked with an Ah Gong, saying, "Most people go and see doctor to collect medicine.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: How come you see doctor, bring medicine to see doctor?" So, he laughed and said, "Doctor asked me what medicine do I take.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, I brought everything there." And I am pretty sure, if I looked into his plastic bag, there would be medicine that has been issued by another doctor many months or even some time ago, and probably had expired.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Today, the Agency for Integrated Care (AIC) under MOH shares data with community health partners to enable them to engage and provide befriending services or care to seniors.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The HIB will provide an additional channel for the sharing of non-NEHR health information to better support national health programmes and initiatives.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Lim has been skipping his polyclinic appointments and struggles to manage his diabetes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Without the opportunity to see Mr Lim, the polyclinic cannot seek his consent to share his contact and relevant health information with community health partners for follow-up.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: However, if our community healthcare providers and their partners are aware of Mr Lim's conditions, they can better support him.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: With the HIB, when Mr Lim's polyclinic assesses that he would benefit from community support, the polyclinic can potentially share his contact information and an indicator of his level of health risk, such as whether he has a chronic condition, with AIC.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: AIC can then prioritise engaging Mr Lim, encourage him to check on his well-being and link him up with necessary support if needed.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: AIC's early engagement of seniors like Mr Lim allows them to benefit from healthcare providers and community-based services before their isolation sets in, leading to more serious health consequences.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And again, this is a scenario that I am sure many Members in the House see when we do our house visits, meeting our seniors in the community, especially seniors living alone, isolated.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And these provisions under the HIB will help to enable better care for our seniors.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To ensure that the Bill addresses Singapore's healthcare needs as well as considers stakeholders' views, MOH has been engaging the public and stakeholders since 2022.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I would also like to thank the professional bodies and healthcare professionals for their feedback, particularly regarding the cyber and data security requirements and the support that their members and colleagues may require as part of the transition.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In the example of Ms Kamala shared earlier, NEHR would only be able to support her new doctor if key health information from her previous healthcare providers were contributed to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As certain public agencies such as the Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) and the Singapore Civil Defence Force (SCDF) also provide patient care, the Bill enables these agencies to be gazetted under the Act to contribute key health information to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Key health information of Singapore Citizens, permanent residents and patients with long-term immigration passes will need to be contributed as these groups are more likely to seek care in Singapore over time.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Health information of transient visitors such as tourists need not be contributed.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Clauses 10 to 15 set out the provisions relating to the contribution of key health information to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The First Schedule lists the key health information that each licensee category needs to contribute, based on the patient care functions they provide.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: NEHR access will be provided to the healthcare providers that are contributing key health information to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Bill will also enable NEHR access for community health partners providing clinical or care planning services.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is in recognition of their increasingly important role in supporting patients' continuity of care.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To enable the provision of timely and effective care, there will not be a need for every healthcare professional to seek consent each time they access their patients' NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: At the same time, we are mindful that patients expect their NEHR information to be kept confidential.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Bill provides for robust legislative safeguards to address these concerns.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We also have in place technical controls to ensure that access to NEHR is tightly regulated.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: NEHR access for patient care purposes will be limited to licensed healthcare providers and their authorised individuals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Healthcare providers must only authorise NEHR access for healthcare professionals who require it for patient care purposes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Such professionals include doctors, nurses, pharmacists and allied health professionals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Individuals who only perform an administrative or corporate role, even if they are healthcare professionals, will not be given NEHR access.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Authorised individuals must access NEHR only for patients whom they are providing patient care to.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Healthcare providers must also implement appropriate practices to ensure their healthcare professionals access NEHR appropriately.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This will include regular training on the appropriate use of NEHR and conducting audits on NEHR access.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In short, access to NEHR is restricted to healthcare professionals for the purpose of providing care to their patients.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This means healthcare professionals will not be allowed to access NEHR for purposes such as filling out medical reports required for insurance claims or pre-employment medical screening forms.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This will address the concerns expressed during the public consultation that health information could be used in a discriminatory manner by employers or insurance companies.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: However, there are medical examinations set out in statutes which serve to protect the public and safeguard the health of the individual and those around him.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Examples include examinations of persons who are at risk of an infectious disease and the medical examinations to assess fitness for service in the SAF, SCDF and Singapore Police Force as required under the Enlistment Act.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: NEHR access will therefore be allowed for these statutory medical examinations.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Clauses 16 to 23 set out the provisions relating to NEHR access, including the legislative safeguards.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Second Schedule sets out the categories of authorised individuals who may access NEHR for different categories of healthcare providers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The specified statutory medical examinations for which NEHR may be accessed is listed in the Third Schedule.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: First, authorised individuals will only be granted access to the data types required for their patient care duties.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, nurses in general will not have access to radiological images as they do not require this information for their patient care duties.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: System-level controls to limit unauthorised access, such as limiting the number of patient records that can be accessed within a stipulated timeframe and conducting regular audits to flag unauthorised NEHR access, have already been implemented.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will be progressively rolling out additional technical measures and processes to limit and detect unauthorised access to NEHR information of patients.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Patients themselves can monitor access of their NEHR information through their HealthHub account and can report suspicious activities to MOH for investigations.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For those who continue to have privacy concerns, they may restrict access to their NEHR information so that only select healthcare providers may have this access.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This Access Restriction feature is like the approach adopted by countries like Australia, Estonia and Hong Kong.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Today, such an Access Restriction regime is already in place.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Patients can submit their request to place an Access Restriction at public healthcare institutions (PHIs).

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For patient safety, when patients visit their healthcare providers, the provider will still be able to view a subset of records in the patients' NEHR even if there is an Access Restriction in place.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This subset of records comprises critical allergies and vaccination information that helps reduce the risk of inappropriate prescriptions or immunisations when patients visit new healthcare providers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Further, a patient's NEHR information may be accessed during medical emergencies despite an Access Restriction.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This feature, known as "break-glass", is like Australia's approach.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Access in such extenuating situations will be subject to strict controls.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Second, before "breaking glass", the doctor must re-verify their credentials and declare a medical emergency has happened.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Third, every instance where a doctor "breaks glass" will be subject to audits.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To ensure there are no gaps in patients' records even during emergencies, health information will continue to be contributed to NEHR even when an Access Restriction is placed.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: While Access Restriction is an option, we do not encourage its use as it would adversely affect the quality of care we receive as patients.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is only when healthcare providers – our doctors and our frontline healthcare staff – have access to our key health information that they can deliver holistic and effective care in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Next, let me turn to clauses 29 to 33, which deal with Access Restrictions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Details relating to these Access Restrictions will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As the national repository of key health information, NEHR information can be used to inform national policies and research to improve population health outcomes for Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, in the event of a major drug contamination incident, MOH may share necessary information from NEHR, such as the identity of patients prescribed with the drug, with relevant healthcare institutions and direct them to promptly contact the affected individuals and advise them to stop taking the drug and seek medical care.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The HIB will not impede the sharing of NEHR information as required or permitted under other laws.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, NEHR information may be required under the Criminal Procedure Code 2010 to facilitate criminal investigations by the Police or by the Communicable Diseases Agency under the Infectious Diseases Act 1976 for outbreak investigations and contact tracing of potentially exposed individuals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But for all requests, MOH will assess whether the NEHR information is appropriate and necessary for the purpose of the request, taking into consideration factors such as whether alternative information is suitable and whether anonymised or aggregated data would suffice.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The sharing of NEHR information under other laws, as well as for public health and public interest purposes, are provided for in clause 5 and clauses 20 to 28 respectively.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: First, data sharing must be between specified entities.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For a start, this will cover key public healthcare stakeholders such as PHIs, AIC and public agencies.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Second, information must only be shared for specified use cases to support continuity of care and population health outreach under national programmes such as Healthier SG and Age Well SG.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, PHIs may share contact information and the addresses of seniors with AIC for AIC to contact and engage these seniors to connect them to relevant community-based care services and activities based on their needs.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Third, we will restrict the data types that can be shared to those relevant to each use case.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The scope and key requirements for the sharing of non-NEHR health information are provided for under clauses 45 to 60 while the use cases and specified entities are set out in the Fourth Schedule.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The list of data types allowed for each use case will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Healthcare providers that contribute to and access NEHR as well as entities allowed to share and receive non-NEHR health information will need to meet cybersecurity and data security requirements.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They will also be responsible for assessing whether a notifiable cybersecurity incident or data breach has occurred.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Once confirmed, MOH will need to be notified.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These security requirements are covered in clauses 61 to 82.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To be clear, today, licensed healthcare providers and practitioners already have obligations to safeguard the personal data of their patients under existing laws.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The security requirements under the HIB are based on existing standards and legal requirements.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: What the HIB does is to consolidate these requirements in relation to health information.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Additionally, the Bill will empower the Minister for Health to take emergency measures in critical events where the threat to health information or relevant health information systems could result in health information being lost or compromised.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Such powers are not unique to this Bill and can be found in the Infectious Diseases Act 1976 and the Cybersecurity Act 2018.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have seen how incidents, whether cyber or physical in nature, can lead to major and prolonged disruptions of essential services around the world, including healthcare services.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Physical incidents, such as fires, can take out information systems and result in data loss, just as faulty information technology (IT) updates or cyberattacks can lead to the same outcome.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Hence, these powers are scoped towards enabling responses to protect health information regardless of the form of the threat.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Should an outage involving health information or the systems that host or process such information occur in Singapore and threaten a major disruption of healthcare services, clauses 83 to 85 will allow the Minister to direct relevant healthcare providers to take mitigating or recovery measures.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This would give healthcare providers sufficient time to familiarise themselves with the Bill’s requirements and strengthen their cybersecurity and data security postures.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MOH is working closely with healthcare providers on the implementation timelines and will announce further details soon.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MOH has been engaging the associations and providers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I wish to reassure them that MOH is committed to supporting them through this transition.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will inform healthcare providers of NEHR-compatible systems that meet the Bill’s cybersecurity requirements and automate the contribution of key health information.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: With the use of such NEHR-compatible systems, healthcare providers will then only need to ensure their data security measures are in place, such as training staff involved in patient care to access and use NEHR appropriately.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Training resources and programmes, as well as funding support, will be made available to support healthcare providers and healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are aware that some healthcare professionals are concerned about increased liability from accessing and using NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MOH is working towards publishing guidelines on the appropriate access and use of NEHR information that healthcare professionals, including nurses and allied health professionals, may use as a resource.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I will now touch on the key offences and the penalties.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Under the HIB, non-compliance with contribution requirements is not an offence in the first instance, as we recognise that there could be genuine challenges onboarding to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: If non-contribution arises from technical difficulties, for instance, we will work with healthcare providers to rectify the underlying issue.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And I reinforce, it is really in the event of deliberate or reckless non-compliance or breaches.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For breaches that are likely to have a greater impact on patients, maximum penalties are higher.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The penalty for this offence is comparable to other relevant laws.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For instance, the maximum fine of $50,000 is aligned with serious breaches involving unauthorised access to computer material in the Computer Misuse Act 1993.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Breaches involving systemic failures are dealt with most severely.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: A failure would likely be committed by a healthcare provider or other organisation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Hence, the maximum fine must be high enough to serve as an effective deterrent to such organisations.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Nevertheless, these are maximum penalties, which are aimed at addressing the most egregious of breaches.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We would like to reassure healthcare providers and healthcare professionals as well as Singaporeans that should potential breaches occur, MOH will look at the facts of each case carefully.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Bill also allows for a range of enforcement actions besides prosecution, including composition of offences, directions to rectify breaches and letters of warning.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Through “One Patient, One Health Summary, One Care Journey”, Singaporeans will benefit from better coordinated care, enhanced quality of care and lower costs.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I urge Members of the House to support the Bill.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Over the last several years, healthcare in Singapore has been on a profound journey of transformation – from hospital to community, from treating sickness to preventing it.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Bill marks a decisive step on that journey.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: At its heart, the HIB is not about technology.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is about enabling a healthcare system that is more connected, more proactive and more centred on the patients, not on institutions.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Health Government Parliamentary Committee (GPC) supports this Bill.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Over the course of this debate, my colleagues will examine it from the perspectives of patients, general practitioners (GPs), allied health professionals, workers, legal safeguards and cybersecurity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We are united by one conviction – this Bill must deliver safer, more continuous and more trusted care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: I will focus on what the Health GPC regards as most critical – continuity of care, especially as care shifts into the community.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They experience it as a journey – often a long one – across GP clinics, polyclinics, hospitals, community hospitals, community health posts, home care teams and social services.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Yet, too often, our systems still treats each encounter as if it were disconnected.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For many of them, especially seniors and those managing chronic conditions, the biggest challenge is not access to care but continuity of care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My Woodlands residents tell me: “I have to repeat my story every time”; or “My GP didn’t know what the hospital had done or that my medication had changed”; or “My mother was discharged, but no one seems to have the full picture.” One of my “Ah Mas" in Woodlands carried a plastic bag stuffed with her medical records – and yes, medications, just like the Senior Minister of State’s resident “Ah Gong” – wherever she went, just in case.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And this is not only about the very old.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Woodlands Hospital is already seeing residents in their 40s and 50s at the Accident and Emergency Department (A&E), presenting with diabetes and complications.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: They bounce between providers, miss follow-ups, have poor disease control and ultimately, fall out of the system.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That is exactly why longitudinal, joined up information matters.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we wait until people are frail, we have already failed them.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Continuity of care is directly linked to public health and early intervention.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: When middle-aged residents presenting with advanced diabetes, it tells us we did not see them early enough, support them consistently enough or connect the dots across years of care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A health information system that allows us to identify patterns – not to police individuals, but to detect communities at risk – gives us the ability to intervene before preventable diseases derail lives.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Continuity of care is not an abstract principle.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is about whether a doctor sees the whole patient, not just the part that walks into their clinic that day.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is the difference between safe medicine and risky medicine, between early prevention and avoidable deterioration.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is foundational to patient safety, quality of care, system efficiency and dignity.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is particularly important in the community setting, where healthcare and social care must operate in close coordination.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This Woodlands project could show what becomes possible when care is joined up, data works for the people and communities lead the way – a model that could inspire the rest of Singapore.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But none of this works if information does not move.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If the GP does not know what medications were changed, if the community nurse does not see the discharge summary, if the social worker is unaware of the medical risks at home, care becomes fragmented.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Residents repeat their histories, tests and procedures may be duplicated, caregivers are left uncertain and opportunities for early intervention are missed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Conversely, when information is shared, care becomes coordinated and outcomes improve.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Residents feel assured, caregivers feel supported and the system functions more effectively.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Bill also enables a learning healthcare system.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With longitudinal data, we can anticipate disease, manage chronic illness better, support public health planning and evidence-based policy-making and accelerate medical research breakthroughs, from early cancer detection to precision or personalised medicine.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: For public health planners, this data allows us to understand which neighbourhoods are ageing faster, where chronic disease is poorly controlled and where caregivers are under strain, so we can deploy resources where they are needed most, not where the voices are loudest.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But none of this can succeed without public trust.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And trust, Sir, is not built by aspiration.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: It is built by rules, limits and accountability.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And that is why the Health GPC will be watching five critical issues closely.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The Bill allows broad categories of “authorised users” to access NEHR data for healthcare and care coordination.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: My residents’ greatest anxieties relate to sensitive data including mental health, reproductive health and social vulnerabilities.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This fear is real, but the solution to fear is not fragmented care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: The solution is stronger rules on who can see what.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Member Alex Yeo, a lawyer, will address this from a legal and governance standpoint while Member David Hoe will bring his characteristic moral framing and empathy for the most vulnerable in our community, that I have come to admire so much in a short time in this House.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: And earlier, in the PSGA debate, Member Cai Yinzhou made the case that when Government agencies and external parties want to use health data for non-healthcare purposes, there must be clear use cases, justifications and safeguards.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Doctors must not be placed in ambiguous positions of having to decide what can or cannot be disclosed, and patients must not be pressured to consent to disclosures that undermine the spirit of the law.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Our labour Member Dr Wan Rizal will speak from the National Trades Union Congress (NTUC) perspective on safeguarding workers' rights – particularly for those with mental health conditions, this is his passion.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Many Woodlands residents have seen the same GP for decades.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Some of these GPs cared for my residents when they were young and are now caring for their children.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Smaller providers often have limited manpower and IT resources.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If onboarding, cybersecurity and reporting requirements are too costly or complex, smaller GPs could struggle.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: We then risk widening the gap between large institutions and community care – exactly the opposite of what this Bill intends.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Financial support, shared services models and practical implementation timelines must be clearly set out.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: MPs Yip Hon Weng, Joan Pereira and Choo Pei Ling will speak on how to support these GP clinics and community partners.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Fourth, protection for doctors and allied health professionals.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Clinical protocols, medico-legal guidance and professional standards must be clear so that healthcare workers are not unfairly exposed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: A doctor himself, Member Dr Hamid Razak, will speak on medico-legal clarity for doctors, while Member Choo Pei Ling together and Member Dr Wan Rizal will speak up for allied healthcare professionals – community nurses, therapists, social workers – who play a critical role in community care and must also have clarity and protection when using NEHR data.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Audit logs, breach detection, structured response and transparent communication to citizens are essential.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Member Yip Hon Weng will address resilience and cybersecurity measures, drawing on perspectives of the Defence GPC.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Members Choo Pei Ling and David Hoe will speak on breach response, transparency and recourse.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Why can't I opt out fully?" We should be honest.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: There are many things in life one can opt out of, but you cannot opt out of safe care.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: In an emergency, your doctor must know your allergies.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: That makes safeguards even more important, not less.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Access to sensitive data must be carefully designed.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Prohibitions on employment and insurance use must be real in practice, not just in statute.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: But our support comes with a. responsibility to ensure continuity of care is delivered in practice, that safeguards are real, professional guidance is clear and that community-based providers are not left behind.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: If we get this right, my Woodlands Ah Ma would no longer need to carry her medical history in her plastic bag.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: Her integrated care team will already have it, working together across settings to give her the best possible care and ensure she enjoys a good quality of life well into her old age.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: This is the system this Bill must deliver.

speaker: Ms Mariam Jaafar (Sembawang)
text: With these expectations clearly in mind, I support the Bill.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It will set the legal framework for the mandatory contribution, collection, storage and disclosure of health information across the entire healthcare ecosystem of Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: When passed, fragmented and often paper-based health records held by individual healthcare providers will be a thing of the past, morphing into a unified interoperable NEHR.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Bill promises smoother, safer, more efficient healthcare for all patients under our country's health system.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Given Singapore's rapidly ageing population, successful implementation of NEHR is critical to ensuring seamless care and continuity across different healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, these benefits come with trade-offs, which, if not properly addressed, will affect the people's trust in this national Smart Nation effort.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: After all, nothing could be more sensitive and personal than one's health information records over the years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The thought of such intimate human data being viewed by viewed by nameless, faceless persons, other than your own doctors, or even worse, falling to the hands of hackers, must be very real to some of us when we contemplate the HIB.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Thus, while I support the Bill, I wish to raise a few concerns posed by the HIB, and I will be speaking on the challenges for smaller healthcare operators, such as single or dual-doctor practitioner clinics that many of my residents rely on for their daily medical needs.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even with strict regulations and legal governance frameworks, there has been cases of unauthorised access as well as outright hacks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is public knowledge that some of the most egregious data breaches in the past 10 years have happened within healthcare.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Chief among them was the 2018 hack of the SingHealth system that led to a Committee of Inquiry, and also the delay of the NEHR roll-out by more than five years.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Till today, the identified hostile state actors behind the attack remain unaccounted for.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More recently, there have been at least two reported cases of unauthorised access by healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For instance, a neurosurgeon at SingHealth was dismissed in 2022 for inappropriately assessing the medical records of over 70 patients not under his care.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More recently, in 2025, a customer service associate at the NUH was found to have unlawfully accessed the records of 11 individuals, including family members and former colleagues via NUHS' internal Epic system, reportedly driven by personal motives to reconnect with one of them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the overwhelming majority of healthcare professionals uphold ethical and legal standards, the ease of access to such records will severely undermine public trust.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Many of us may be asking how can I be sure that the GP clinic at the next block to mine with only one and half doctors, and one to two doctors and two clinic staff on shifts be able to comply with the HIB and also be self-protected against cyber and data risk created by either human or system errors.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The NEHR is only as secure as the smallest operators are.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the HIB's stringent requirements are essential for safeguarding patient data and access, they place a significant burden on smaller healthcare providers who may no longer opt out of contribution to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Large institutions like SingHealth and National Health Group may mobilise their dedicated IT teams.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Small practices, however, will find themselves in unfamiliar territory and will have to rely on costly external consultants to comply, creating a significant operational burden.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On an ongoing basis, the challenge is particularly acute when it comes to warding off attacks and data breaches.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Under the law, healthcare providers of all sizes share legal liability for data breaches caused by health data intermediary failure, placing a disproportionate burden on clinics that lack control over these risks.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Small healthcare operators may be out pocket for purposes of upgrading and maintaining their clinic management systems to meet strict security standards, audit trails and data portability.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Even with this grant, GPs are simply not trained to assess whether their providers use genuine end-to-end encryption, secure server configurations, or follow basic cyber security best practices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How can we help clinics to use appropriately secure yet affordable compliance systems?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How can we ensure the essential cyber hygiene practices like staff training and regular software updates are undertaken without imposing disproportionate cost burden and/or adding to the existing pressures of running their small practices?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should also be concerned whether this leads to GPs passing the cost down to patients and reducing affordability in primary care.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How will MOH ensure that such cost will not be passed down to patients?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: How will it affect our mom-and-pop clinics and family doctors?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They are an important part of keeping us safe and healthy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: With the Community Health Assist Scheme (CHAS) and Healthier SG schemes, they have become more integrated into the overall health delivery infrastructure nationwide – at least some of them.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: However, they are often by nature very small, akin to mom-and-pop clinics, often fronted by one doctor with, say, possibly another on a locum basis, or not even without another locum, they open only part of the day.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Some may not even have air conditioning and some may still use paper records.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, the doctors are older, serving their patients past their official retirement age, which makes them well loved and trusted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I do wonder whether the passing of the HIB with punitive costs for non-participation and compliance may be the straw that breaks this group and push them to give up their practices for good.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I certainly hope not, even if they are in a minority.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We should be concerned about conveniently located medical services disappearing from our neighbourhoods at exactly the point when Singapore is becoming a super-aged society that needs more care, not less.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A volunteer shared with me recently her worries for her 87-year-old mother who lives in her own flat and is under the trusted care of her family doctor a few blocks away.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This doctor runs a solo practice in a void deck shop without air-conditioning.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: He only opens a few hours a day, but this suits the elderly patients that he mostly serves.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: If this doctor is forced to close due to implementation of the HIB, my volunteer is worried that her mother will no longer have convenient access to care.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It will be stressful for this volunteer as a daughter living away from her mother whenever her mother falls ill, needs to top up her medicines or take a vaccination, whereas currently, she trusts her mom to visit this doctor and her troubles will usually be sorted.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, extend financial support beyond GP IT Enablement Grant and set up an IT Shared Services Office.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This may be an extension of the GP IT Enablement Grant, but targeted towards the smaller operators rather than the chain clinics.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They need Institute of Technical Education technicians to help them directly when issues arise.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: To address this, could the Minister consider setting up an IT Shared Services Office within the Ministry that may provide small clinics with not a one-off, but a continuing out-sourced, cost effective and compliant IT support, acting in lieu of the dedicated IT department of large healthcare institutions?

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Besides my suggestion above, I would also urge MOH to consider setting up a similar initiative to support all clinics and practices, like the shared services initiative for charities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The Commissioner of Charities has partnered with various organisations to set up shared services to strengthen charities, regulatory compliance and efficiency of their backend operations, especially helpful to smaller charities.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This Bill changes the rules of the game.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It mandates that every private clinic from the specialist in Orchard Road to the void deck GP in the heartlands must contribute their data.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They have no choice if they wish to stay open.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But if MOH were to demand institution-grade security against risk and breaches on a solo operator's budget, it may not just be unfair, it may even be unsustainable for some.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Compliance with the HIB cannot be a one-size-fits-all assignment.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More must be done to help onboard small clinics and family doctors at the same level of standards and readiness as large institutions.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Let us not make the small clinics the weakest link of the system.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: They should also be the trusted mission-critical partners, worthy of a Smart Nation.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Next, Mr Deputy Speaker, in the final part of my speech, I will touch on the penalty regime under the HIB.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: I have spoken about the SingHealth data breach of 2018.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: While the figure of $1,000,000 appears substantial in isolation, it pales when contextualised against the scale of modern healthcare data breaches, such as the SingHealth one in 2018.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Let us do the math: 1.5 million SingHealth records were leaked in 2018.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: A total fine of $1 million – $750,000 plus $250,000 – equates to an effective fine per record of 66 Singapore cents.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Furthermore, for a large healthcare conglomerate with annual revenues in the hundreds of million, a $1 million fine is a relatively lesser or even trivial operating expenses.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Relatively speaking, it is roughly equivalent to the cost of a few high-end medical devices.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It is hardly a pain point to some, even less of a serious business risk to the large hospital groups.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Instead, the $1 million cap effectively puts a ceiling on the value of the collective privacy of the nation, regardless of the number of persons attached or affected.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: Let us compare this with global standards that have successfully shifted corporate behaviour.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The 4% turnover clause is the main deterrent.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: For a tech giant or a global hospital chain, this could amount to hundreds of millions or billions of dollars.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This scales the penalty to the size of the entity, ensuring that the fine is never just a cost of doing business.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This directly monetises the harm to the individual.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It creates a mathematical certainty of catastrophe for negligence.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: The penalty, in a sense, may better match the pain of the victims.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: More importantly, it will make organisations take the message much more seriously.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: On the other hand, some may argue that they can better match the pain of the victims.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We can, and perhaps we should, review and decide where the balance may better lie for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: But it is important that our regime must ultimately make all organisations take the message more seriously.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It forces senior management and boards director to view cybersecurity not as an IT cost, but as an existential business risk.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It signals that the state values each individual's privacy.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: It moves away from the abstract notion of system security to the concrete value of personal data.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: This is how we can build a system that is robust at the outset.

speaker: Mr Dennis Tan Lip Fong (Hougang)
text: We can start looking numerically at what would be a good balance for Singapore, or at least a better balance than what we have now, and which pertinently will make all organisations take the message more seriously, while being fair and equitable for bigger medical organisations, as well as smaller clinics and practices.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Their concern is much simpler, it is much more human, and they ask: can this information be used against me?

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I hear this from workers, from our seniors and from caregivers alike.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many residents, especially older residents managing long-term conditions, worry about who can see their information, whether consent is meaningful and what happens if something goes wrong.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These are legitimate concerns and I know that other Members will raise them in detail, particularly on system safeguards and patient protections.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It intersects very directly with their livelihoods, with hiring decisions, job retention, access to work opportunities and sometimes, continued participation in the workforce.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This applies not only to traditional employees, but also to self-employed persons and platform workers, whose access to work can be more fragile and more easily withdrawn.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: In these contexts, the imbalance of power is real.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When income and job security are at stake, workers often feel they have little room to refuse disclosure, even when they are uncomfortable.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is central to whether workers trust the system at all.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Some may ask why this needs emphasis, since the safeguard is already existing in the Bill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The reason is not legal, it is behavioural.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Even the perception that health data could affect employment decisions can discourage workers from seeking timely care, disclosing relevant information to healthcare professionals or participating fully in national health initiatives like Healthier SG.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This would undermine the very objectives of this Bill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Workers should never have to weigh their health against their livelihood.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: If this Bill is to succeed in improving continuity of care and public health outcomes, workers must feel safe engaging with the healthcare system, without fear of downstream consequences at work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This concern is especially relevant for protected characteristics and disabilities, including mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I want to be clear: I am not suggesting that any one type of health condition is more important than another, but from a workplace fairness perspective, some types of information are more likely to be misunderstood, stigmatised or misinterpreted in employment contexts.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Mental health conditions, for example, are often less visible, episodic and poorly understood in workplaces, despite progress over the years.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is the risk of unfair treatment if such information is misused or even informally taken into account.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: This is precisely why the employment-use safeguard is so important.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: The Labour Movement has long stood for the principle that workers should not be discriminated against, on the basis of protected characteristics, including disabilities and mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It reinforces, in the context of health data, the same values we have already affirmed as a society: that personal characteristics and health conditions should not become barriers to fair treatment at work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Seen in this light, this safeguard is not an additional demand.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It is a logical extension of principles that Parliament has already endorsed.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Workers are also concerned about indirect or "backdoor" use of health information.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Not necessarily through access to records, but through fitness-for-work assessments, third-party requirements or other channels that could influence employment outcomes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: I note that the Bill identifies specific Statutory Medical Examinations where NEHR access is permitted, such as pre-enlistment checkups or assessments for vocational driving licenses.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Furthermore, while healthcare providers can override an individual's "Access Restriction" during a medical emergency, the law must remain clear, that data can still never be used for employment purposes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Healthcare workers occupy a unique position in this Bill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They are entrusted to access and handle sensitive health data, they are required to do so as part of patient care, and often times, under pressure and subject to, of course, significant penalties if things go wrong.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: From a labour perspective, safeguards must protect not only patients, but also the workers tasked with implementing the system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Accountability is important and wilful misuse of data must be dealt with firmly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: But accountability must be fair and also proportionate.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: We must distinguish clearly between intentional wrongdoing, and inadvertent errors arising from system design, workflow complexity, or even operational constraints.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: And this means we need to have clear role-based access, proper training and guidance, and supportive implementation, especially during transition periods.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Protecting patient data and treating our healthcare workers fairly are not competing objectives.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They must go hand in hand if the system is to function well.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Many seniors manage multiple conditions and interact frequently within the healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: They worry about privacy, they worry about consent and they worry about whether their personal information is respected.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: While I have focused today on worker trust, I want to assure residents that their concerns are also heard.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: Trust is the common thread, whether one is a worker, a patient, or a caregiver or a senior managing long-term care.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When Singaporeans trust that their health information is handled with care, strong safeguards and clear boundaries, they are more willing to seek care, share information honestly, and participate fully in our healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In Malay):   This Bill must be able to establish public trust.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: No worker should fear that seeking medical care could be held against them at work.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: These safeguards align with principles of fairness and dignity in the workplace, including for individuals with disabilities or mental health conditions.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When trust is maintained, workers and senior citizens will feel more confident in seeking treatment and sharing health information honestly.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: A robust healthcare system begins with trust, and trust only exists when clear boundaries and robust safeguards are implemented.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: (In English): Mr Deputy Speaker, with the right safeguards in place, this Bill can strengthen healthcare delivery and public health outcomes.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: It aligns with long-standing principles against discrimination and it supports, rather than undermines the objectives of this Bill.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: At the end of the day, a healthcare system can only be as strong as the confidence people.

speaker: Dr Wan Rizal (Jalan Besar)
text: When workers, patients and seniors trust that their health data will not be misused, at work or elsewhere, they are more likely to engage, participate and benefit.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is the deeply personal and sensitive, and a digital diary of our physical and mental lives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, the public's trust is sacrosanct to the implementation of the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must ensure that the Government and healthcare stakeholders do their utmost to safeguard the privacy of this data.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I broadly agree with the principles of the HIB, which delineates the responsibilities of our healthcare ecosystem and mandates data contribution, I believe it is also important that we continue to strengthen areas of data privacy, transparency and individual agency.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As we move towards Smart Nation, we must ensure that our progress does not leave Singaporeans feeling as to the power asymmetry between themselves and the state is growing, and that they are losing control of their own data and privacy, and that public education measures would be stepped up to foster a deeper understanding of the NEHR's and one's rights as patients.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: One crucial aspect of this Bill is that patients of opt in or out of the NEHR by way of an Access Restriction, which blocks medical practitioners from viewing all of the patient's NEHR's records, save important details, such as one's critical allergies and personal information.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Patients may also select the medical institutions to the impose and access restriction on.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This, according to MOH, is in the interest of ensuring the expeditious provision of care should the patient wish to opt-in to the NEHR in the future or during an emergency situation.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But Mr Deputy Speaker, if a citizen says "no" to the NEHR today, should the state then be allowed to say, "Okay, but trust me" and collect their data anyway?

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In a 2017 letter to MOH, the then President of the Singapore Medical Association highlighted that this might compromise the patients' right to privacy.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is because patients might not wish for their medical records to be uploaded to the NEHR at all.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I urge the Government to reconsider this continuous background uploading and if other additional options can also be considered.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For example, we should consider offering a total opt out or a so-called "no means no" option, provided the patient is thoroughly briefed on the dangers and risks of doing so and is counselled on the implications of such an option.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Second, patients might prefer to block access to certain documents and records only, instead of imposing a wholesale access restriction on their records.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I understand that one sensitive health information that could potentially lead to stigmatisation and discrimination will be secured by additional measures, such as double lock-in feature.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Nevertheless, what is sensitive to one might not be sensitive to another.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Hence, patients might wish for additional flexibility when protecting their health records rather than just give a blanket nod.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Part 3 of the Bill also allows for the sharing of both administrative and clinical information, to facilitate the continuity of care and outreach efforts for national health programmes through data sharing arrangements.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, I hope that patients will be recorded some flexibility and control over the types of health information they wish to disclose and how they would like that information to be used.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: While I appreciate that we can already check out any NEHR access history in HealthHub, patient consent should also be sought for data sharing between healthcare providers and public agencies.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: On that note, Part 2, Division 4 of the Bill also sets out the requirements for the usage of any NEHR data for secondary purposes or derived information.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: After all, a national health record database provides a valuable snapshot of our population's health condition, which could then be used by researchers for developing solutions to public health issues faced by our society.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The Bill separates such derived information into two categories.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I agree with clause 25(2) that the Minister may approve an application to obtain Type 2 derived information, if the Minister is satisfied, having regard to the purpose for which the application is made.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: That is in the public interest to do so.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Although the cost to the patient's privacy may be outweighed by the benefits such research brings to society at large, that should not preclude the Government from giving patients more agency over secondary usage of the health information, especially for research purposes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This is a principle that is adopted by other healthcare systems worldwide as well.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Therefore, I hope that the Government would consider allowing patients to exercise greater control over the secondary usage of their health data.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To follow on the Ministerial approval requirement under clause 25, according to MOH's Trusted Research and Real World-Data Utilisation and Sharing Tech (TRUST) platform, which provides anonymised healthcare-related data for secondary usage, the Data Access Committee reviews the social value and public interests of each data request.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I agree that access to any NEHR data unlocks research and development (R&D) potential and supports long-term public health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: When it comes to commercial-linked entities, however, while such parties might use the data for generating public health reasons and research, it raises ethical concerns surrounding transparency and privacy, especially if access to data is excessive, insufficiently justified or beyond stated that be used.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: The access was used for monitoring software for mobile devices called Streams which promises to improve clinicians' ability to support patients with acute kidney injury.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: But according to the study's authors, the publicist dated in the agreement were far less specific and made more open-ended references to using data to improve services.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: In the last few years, there has been a significant drive and race across providers to train AI models using the largest and most diverse datasets available in order to achieve better performance.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: However, this trend also raises important concerns about data privacy, particularly, in regard to sensitive records, such as medical information – NEHR data.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: For this reason, we should exercise caution before granting third parties, especially if they are commercially-linked organisations, with excessive or unconstrained access to NEHR data, especially when longitudinal studies examining individuals' health records over prolonged periods are involved and be mindful of scope creep, given commercial incentives.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Besides R&D applications, I do believe that Government should capitalise on the NEHR's capabilities to boost the efficiency of healthcare delivery and financial assistance to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: With allied health professionals, such as medical social workers having access to the patient's NEHR record, I hope that the possibility of financial assistance being further streamlined via enhanced data sharing procedures with the likes of the Social Services Office can be explored – with the patient's approval, of course.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: This would be most helpful in cases, such as long-term assistance to those permanently unable to work due to illness or disability.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And in turn, this could also help to alleviate the workload of our medical social workers while easing the experience of those seeking financial and social support.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: As shared in the Feedback Report on the Public Consultation for the Health Information Bill, during the public consultation exercise, MOH received feedback requesting for a greater clarity and clearer communication of the policy positions under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: It is nonetheless critical that the Government ramp up its patient's education efforts regarding the purposes of the NEHR and how it might benefit them as well as to explain the rights of each patient pertaining to their medical data.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: Medical information is among the most intimate forms of data one can share and the success of the NEHR ultimately depends, not on compulsion, but on trust.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: To ensure this trust is not eroded by a perceived power asymmetry between the state and the individual, we must move beyond a "collect first, tell later" approach.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: And throughout my speech, I have highlighted three recurring themes: agency, transparency and proportionality.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: I hope Singaporeans can be granted more meaningful control and disclosure over how their health information is accessed, shared and used.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: More importantly, we cannot have a well-functioning healthcare system if only 15% of people fully understood what the NEHR is.

speaker: Mr Chua Kheng Wee Louis (Sengkang)
text: We must ramp up public education to ensure every Singaporean knows their rights and how their data is used to serve the common good, in order to foster the trust that turns our national database into a national asset.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Despite Healthier SG, care is not yet delivered in one place or coordinated by one healthcare team.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It moves across clinics, hospitals and community settings.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In such a system, information is not just paperwork.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Because health information accompanies us through our most vulnerable moments, the success of this Bill will not be judged only by how efficiently data flows.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It will be judged by something far more human – whether residents continue to trust the system enough to seek care early, speak honestly and return when they need help.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That trust is fragile and once lost, it is hard to restore.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Today, I would like to focus my clarifications on three areas which residents have consistently raised with me: access control, support for smaller GP clinics and cybersecurity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill introduces Access Restrictions under clause 29, with exceptions in clause 30, and the process for managing them in clause 31.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But residents ask a practical question – will this protect me in real life?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My first question relates to the default setting.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will seniors, especially those who are not digitally confident, know what to do?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If privacy depends on digital literacy, then privacy is no longer equal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: My second question concerns granularity and role-based access.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This is a powerful provision, but power lies in how it is used.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will this flexibility translate into true "need-to-know" access or will residents experience it as broad visibility once someone is authorised?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Access should follow purpose and visibility should follow necessity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Yio Chu Kang residents tell me plainly that they want help, but fear being labelled.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They worry not only about what is written, but about who might see it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This concern extends beyond mental health to other sensitive data such as human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) status, sexually transmitted infections, reproductive health history, genetic conditions and substance use treatments.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: These are conditions where fear of exposure can deter people from seeking care altogether.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents also raise a related fear that goes beyond stigma.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They worry about where boundaries are drawn beyond direct care, such as access by insurers, employers, ancillary service providers or the downstream use of data for research, analytics or artificial intelligence (AI) training.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even where data is described as de-identified, residents worry about re-identification risks and inference.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If these boundaries are not clear and credible, residents may hold back information or delay care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will MOH use the flexibility in clause 29 to ensure such sensitive categories are treated with particular care?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Furthermore, under clause 30, where exceptions allow information to remain accessible, how will MOH ensure these exceptions are narrow and clearly defined rather than quietly eroding the intent of the restriction?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Sensitive care must feel safe or people will stay away.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Healthcare for stigmatised conditions must be a sanctuary, not a spotlight.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Even when information is restricted, residents worry that the very presence of a "sealed" marker invites speculation.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will MOH prevent the fact of restriction itself from becoming a source of stigma or inference?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents can view access logs on HealthHub, which is a good start.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But do they merely see that an organisation has accessed their data or do they understand why?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Beyond investigation timelines, what happens if misuse occurs?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will residents be notified promptly, given a clear explanation and told what corrective or remedial actions have been taken?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In estates like Yio Chu Kang, the neighbourhood GP clinic is not just a provider, it is a relationship where trust has been built over years.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: While the Bill places necessary obligations on institutions, the compliance costs land hardest on these small practices.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: We hear feedback that NEHR can be cluttered and time consuming for less digitally savvy, elderly GPs.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If clinicians spend more time searching and less time caring, have we truly improved care?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Cybersecurity and data requirements designed for large institutions can overwhelm small practices where the doctor is also the administrator and IT troubleshooter.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Some GPs have shared a quiet concern that if requirements become too complex or costly, retirement may be the only option.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When small clinics close, residents, especially seniors, lose convenient access and familiar doctors.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Has MOH weighed this risk against the Bill's policy objectives?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we ask neighbourhood clinics to operate like large corporations, we should not be surprised if they struggle.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents will feel this quickly through higher fees and longer waits.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In that context, I ask whether support will be predictable and sustained.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
