text: Will there be grace periods, phased onboarding and a genuine "no wrong door" approach so small clinics are guided rather than penalised as they come on board?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will responsibility for implementation be clear rather than fragmented?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Where alternative contribution pathways are provided for pen-and-paper clinics, how will MOH ensure these are feasible and not a second-class solution?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Compliance should not become a hidden healthcare tax on the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: For residents, a breach is not a statistic, it is personal.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The 2018 SingHealth cyberattack was a stark reminder that even well-resourced systems are vulnerable.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: As the Chair of the GPC for Defence, I approach this with particular care.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In defence, we learn that systems rarely fail at the centre.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: They fail at the edges, where resources are thin and the smallest gap becomes the point of entry.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: The Bill rightly imposes duties under clause 68 for reasonable safeguards and clause 70 for incident management.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: But residents ask two fundamental questions: will it be secure and will it be doable?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will small clinics have a clear, achievable baseline while larger institutions shoulder proportionately greater responsibility?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: How will MOH support small clinics in meeting incident management requirements under clause 70 without turning doctors into cybersecurity managers?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Will there be shared services, templates, guided exercises and clear escalation pathways so bureaucratic demands do not take doctors away from patients?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Residents also care deeply about what happens when things go wrong.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Where cybersecurity failures arise from vendors or intermediaries, how will accountability follow control so that small clinics are not unfairly blamed or penalised for failures beyond their technical reach?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: When systems are down, patients are at risk.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: What resilience standards will apply to NEHR access?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: A system is only as strong as its weakest link and in healthcare, patients bear the cost of weakness.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: In a super-aged society, care no longer sits in one place, with one doctor, at one time.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Where care moves, trust must move with it.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is about data, but more importantly, it is about people.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about whether access controls feel like protection or complexity.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about whether neighbourhood clinics are strengthened or quietly strained.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: It is about whether cybersecurity inspires confidence or quiet fear.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: At its heart, this Bill asks a deeper question of us as a society.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: Can we build a system that is effective without being intrusive, secure without being crushing and connected without losing compassion?

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: If we get this right, we will not only improve care, we will preserve dignity, we will strengthen trust, and we will send a clear message to every resident – seeking care will never mean surrendering control.

speaker: Mr Yip Hon Weng (Yio Chu Kang)
text: That is the standard we should hold ourselves to.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is in line with the vision of "One Patient, One Health Record", when the NEHR commenced a decade ago.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I understand that patient records from our public healthcare institutions are already in the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Let us say that you sought treatment in the Singapore General Hospital (SGH), information about your visit, such as your admission and discharge records, your laboratory test results, the procedures you did, the medication you were prescribed, are already in the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is significant since one of the reasons why patients opt for private healthcare is so that their health information is not included in the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This is especially concerning for patients dealing with sensitive medical issues, including those related to mental health, sexual health or addiction.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, the success of the NEHR hinges on fostering trust that the Government can collect and consolidate our health information safely and responsibly.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The trust can only exist if we keep patient privacy and patient autonomy at the forefront.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: By patient privacy, I mean that patients must have the assurance that their confidential health data remains private and secure, with access granted only to particular persons for what is medically necessary or for public health purposes.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Patient autonomy, on the other hand, means that patients should be able to meaningfully determine who has access to their data and how their data is used.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: In general, patients should be able to know when and why their data is accessed and by whom.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I believe the Government can agree with me that the NEHR must leave patients feeling empowered, not exposed.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For that to happen, we cannot compromise on either patient privacy or patient autonomy.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, I want to focus on the category of visit diagnosis, reasons for visit, or patient problem list, which many healthcare providers are mandated to contribute.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: How lengthy or extensive should the contribution pertaining to diagnosis, reasons for visit or patient problem list be for the purposes of the NEHR?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I also want to note that, as of 8 January, the "Frequently Asked Questions" (FAQ) on Synapxe's website – Synapxe being our national HealthTech agency responsible for running the NEHR – states that the NEHR is meant to receive and consolidate key health summary information, but "not doctor's notes".

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Let us say a person were to meet a private psychiatrist and discuss their recent psychological difficulties, due to a recent breakdown in his or her marriage.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: The psychiatrist then records these details in their own doctor's notes.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My first question: when contributing health information to the NEHR about the visit, is the psychiatrist mandated to include those personal and private details of the patient's life under the category of "visit diagnoses, reasons for visit or patient problem list"?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: My second question: if the private psychiatrist was not mandated to share their doctor's notes, can such information still be contributed to the NEHR, including without the patient's knowledge?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I believe that the public will benefit from an assurance from the Ministry that the scope of health information contained in the NEHR will only relate to key health summary data and will not include "doctor’s notes", especially intimate and confidential details about a patient's personal life, even if that information were in some way medically relevant to the provision of care.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I am sure that all patients appreciate the assurance that their healthcare information cannot be used for employment and insurance purposes.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: However, I want to ask the Minister whether the Police and other law enforcement agencies will be similarly barred from using information from the NEHR?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: For instance, if a substance abuser sought treatment on his own to battle his addiction, would law enforcement be able to use the NEHR records to arrest and charge him?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I ask this because patients seek treatment and care with some expectation of confidentiality, that their sensitive health information will be kept private.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: We need to ensure that patients continue to feel comfortable to seek treatment.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Clauses 29 and 30 allow for access restrictions, which patients can use either to restrict all access to their information in the NEHR or to restrict access for specific users or purposes.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: And if I understand clause 30(7) correctly, these Class 1 and Class 2 access restrictions do not prevent or restrict the contribution of healthcare information by a medical provider.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Currently, there is an option to opt out of the NEHR, but this involves a slightly elaborate and tedious process of making an appointment at one of the polyclinics and restructured hospitals to obtain and submit an opt-out form.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: What happens is that healthcare providers do not get to view them.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, these Access Restrictions can be, understandably, overridden in a medical emergency.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I thus want to ask how the Ministry intends to implement the Access Restriction mechanisms under the Bill.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Thirdly, is the Ministry planning to conduct regular public campaigns to educate patients about their access restriction rights?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I understand that patients can view which healthcare providers have accessed their health records through the NEHR Access History section in HealthHub.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I want to clarify with the Minister about how granular this data would be.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Would the patient only be able to see which healthcare institutions have accessed their records or will it also list out the specific healthcare professionals who were accessing their records?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, at GP clinics, how can patients be sure that only their doctor is able to view the health information on the NEHR and not their non-clinical staff?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This relates to another question about unauthorised access to the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Would it not be more reasonable, not to mention the right thing to do, to notify affected individuals in any and all cases of unauthorised access to their health information?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Looking ahead, the national electronic healthcare system, once it is fully up and running, our citizen's pooled health data will be a valuable goldmine for clinical researchers and pharmaceutical companies.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: While this can accelerate drug development and spur medical innovation, the public needs assurance that their personal health data will not be monetised for profit.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Here, my question is whether the Government intends to make healthcare information in the NEHR available to the private, academic or any other sectors and whether the current Bill makes provisions to regulate such a possibility?

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Moreover, if the data is used for commercial research, the Government should consider a "Social Dividend" which ensures that the benefits return to the people.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: Any revenue or benefits derived should be reinvested directly into patient subsidies or national health funds, ensuring that the value generated by the people's health data is returned back to the people.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: I would also suggest exploring the model of data cooperatives.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: One example of this model is non-profit Swiss cooperative MIDATA where citizens control their data and can choose to contribute it to specific research projects that they believe in.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: This has enabled research and tailored care plans for diseases, such as multiple sclerosis.

speaker: Mr Fadli Fawzi (Aljunied)
text: To this end, we continue to emphasise patients' privacy and patients' autonomy to ensure Singaporeans are empowered, not exposed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Before I start, I wish to declare that as a legal practitioner in private practice, I have and do act for insurers and insureds in a variety of disputes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In many urgent and emergency medical situations, this could certainly save lives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: On the other hand, the Bill also incorporates safeguards, a reflection that in this tech pervasive information age, personal healthcare information, in the wrong hands, used for inappropriate and insidious purposes, can potentially destroy lives.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As we expand the NEHR to include all healthcare providers in Singapore, invariably, the number of access points to the NEHR will increase significantly.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Any digital online system with many access points is particularly vulnerable to unauthorised access, inappropriate use and/or a cyber threat.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The Bill incorporates stringent access rules and restrictions, with deterrent penalties for breaches.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Individuals are also at liberty to place access restrictions and view instances of NEHR access to their medical records via the HealthHub App.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The Bill therefore provides safeguards while giving individuals with privacy concerns to decide on who should have access rights.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I am therefore glad to hear from the Senior Minister of State that MOH will conduct regular audits to flag inappropriate access to the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This is vital as it will provide healthcare providers regular and crucial information and feedback on the strength of their protocols and processes and allow them to act in a timely manner to adjust and tighten as required.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Given the large number of healthcare providers in Singapore, I would like to invite the Senior Minister of State to share with the House, the Ministry's plans on how these audits would be conducted, including the frequency and parameters of what would be studied, to ensure that the safeguards remain robust and amply protect the personal healthcare information of Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: I now move on to the point on consent.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The notion of patient consent is fundamental in medical practice – serving as a cornerstone in both legal and ethical obligations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Doctors regularly seek patient agreement in instances, such as treatment/interventions or to share medical information with a third party, including family members and so on.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Even in the case where a patient has lost mental capacity, legal documents, such as a Lasting Power of Attorney or the legal appointment of a deputy, authorises another to, in effect, "consent" on the patient’s behalf.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In the context of healthcare, patient involvement in decisions about their care is an intuitive concept.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In fact, it makes it compulsory for healthcare providers to do so.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This can be a cause for concern for Singaporeans who may legitimately have privacy concerns with uploading their personal healthcare records onto the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: One may ask, why can I not choose not to upload my healthcare information onto the NEHR?

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: This is especially so since the harm or detriment suffered would likely be largely to the individual in the event of a leak or misuse.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: We have also appeared to have taken a slightly different approach from jurisdictions, such as Australia, which allows patients to choose whether or what medical records to upload onto their system which is called "My Health Record" or to even have a record at all.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: As I believe, this would be an issue of interest to many Singaporeans, I invite the Senior Minister of State to share the policy and practical considerations behind why the framework governing the NEHR has been set up in this manner.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Clause 6 of the Bill sets out excluded purposes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In other words, these are purposes for which healthcare providers are not allowed to access the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Speaking from professional experience, it is important to have a clear demarcation of what relevant medical information of individuals should be provided in the context of these employer/employee and insurer/insured relationships, and what is sensitive confidential medical information that could be misinterpreted or inappropriately applied.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Individuals should not be compelled to allow access for such purposes.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: For example, if all insurers in Singapore require NEHR access consent before agreeing to cover an individual under a health-related policy, then the individual is left with no real choice but to agree if he or she wants to be covered by the insurance.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: However, I believe that there is a case to be made to allow for some relevant healthcare information to be accessed.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Let us take the example of a health-related insurance policy.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Generally, an insurer decides on whether to extend cover and if so, set the premium payable based on actuarial calculations.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: These calculations take into account a number of factors, including pre-existing medical conditions and medical history.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: If individuals can consent to a limited scope of relevant information that is agreed between the patient and in this instance, the insurer, then access can be permitted for that limited scope of relevant information via the healthcare provider.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: It may be useful to understand whether this would impact insurance premium setting and/or insurance cover in the future, if and when the Bill comes into effect.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: There is also, an instance in which the blanket exclusion can be lifted.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Before I conclude, I just want to make one observation of Mr Dennis Tan’s suggestion to increase the penalties for a breach.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: The balance, however, in such matters is between taking a punitive approach or supportive approach, where we work with healthcare providers to strengthen their protocols and processes in order to prevent breaches to re-occur.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Mr Tan makes the point that large organisations may take financial penalties as a cost of business.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: In some cases, this may very well be true.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: However, in the case of a healthcare provider, the people within – clinicians, nurses, administrators and so on – are well intentioned and want to build a system that better serves patients.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: When such a breach incident happens, I believe, it impacts not only the organisation but also the personal professional reputations of the people involved.

speaker: Mr Alex Yeo (Potong Pasir)
text: Viewed from this context, a punitive approach may not be the best option.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A population-scale set of longitudinal medical records is the "means of production" for more timely interventions, accurate diagnoses and preventive health at large.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The contribution of data to the NEHR will create a valuable dataset and that value should flow to all Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But before I move on to the question of value, my belief is that a Bill that compels contribution must also come with robust ecosystem safeguards.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: From my conversations with practitioners and from my reading of the Bill, I have three sets of concerns: (a) the disproportionate cybersecurity burden on small providers; (b) the uploading of sensitive medical information despite patient objections; and (c) possible insurance loopholes that may render our privacy protections ineffective.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I will then speak to a broader question: if we are building a national health asset, who benefits and how do we continue to ensure it catalyses a dynamic ecosystem rather than becoming captured by a single monopoly provider?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: First, to the cybersecurity obligations imposed on healthcare providers.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Bill designates all Healthcare Services Act licensees – from tertiary hospitals employing thousands to single-doctor GP clinics in HDB heartlands – as "relevant persons" under section 64.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: All face the same statutory obligations: to implement reasonable controls for secure processing, reasonable safeguards against unauthorised access and cybersecurity protections under sections 66 and 68.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Bill does use the word "reasonable", which implies proportionality.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But I have spoken with doctors who run small operations.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They worry that when a breach occurs – and breaches are a matter of "when" and not "if" – the enforcement spotlight will fall on them.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I also wish to speak for some of my constituents who are senior GPs still practising in the heartlands.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Many are approaching retirement and are not tech-savvy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: They will struggle with the digitalisation requirements that this Bill will impose.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If the transition is too abrupt, many of these senior GPs may feel forced to retire early or sell their independent clinics to large corporate chains, accelerating consolidation in the primary care sector.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The end state of a modern, integrated health information system is desirable.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, I ask: one, would the Ministry issue clear, tiered guidance on what constitutes "reasonable" safeguards for practices of different sizes?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Two, will the Ministry consider providing or subsidising cybersecurity insurance for small providers so that they need not fear shouldering the entire financial risk of a breach?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Three, will there be a transition period with educational enforcement, rather than immediate punitive action, to allow smaller providers to build up cybersecurity capabilities?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Four, could the Ministry offer transitional support for senior practitioners nearing retirement, perhaps something as simple as sending personnel to help digitalise their records monthly?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, to the question of sensitive medical conditions that patients wish to keep private.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: There is a group of patients today who pay cash, wanting to keep their records, perhaps with sexually transmitted infections, mental health conditions or abortion records, off the system.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Many foreigners also do not want to be on NEHR.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Under this Bill, that option will no longer exist.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It does not exclude the data from NEHR.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If the burden of proof is on the custodian of NEHR to have a robust privacy model, let us examine the custodian.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The Committee of Inquiry found that IHiS staff lacked adequate cybersecurity awareness, that key staff failed to take appropriate action even when there were clear signs of an ongoing attack, and that the Chief Information Security Officer's response was, and I quote, "clearly lacking and displayed an alarming lack of concern”.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This has led many doctors to mistrust Synapxe in these matters.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Given the history here, I believe our health authorities also need to take steps towards rebuilding that trust.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, I ask: one, how is MOH going to police unjustified access of NEHR, where rogue elements read medical histories of unrelated people?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: What assurance can MOH give us that our health data is safe with Synapxe?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Two, if such unauthorised access occurs, does proactive monitoring exist or will the system rely solely on whistle-blowers and complaints?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Three, what is the technical architecture for access-restricted data?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Or is it simply flagged in the same database, such that a breach would expose it alongside unrestricted records?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Four, what is the access model for NEHR data?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This dual authorisation prevents rogue access because no single party can retrieve records alone.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Will Singapore's NEHR access model include such safeguards?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And five, what is MOH’s position on specific carve-outs for defined sensitive conditions, where patients can opt out of contribution entirely?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: According to section 3.1.2.2 of the Draft Guidelines on Appropriate Use and Access to NEHR, released by MOH in 2023: "In the event that such information was previously transcribed from NEHR into the patient's clinical notes, it would be treated as part and parcel of the medical record belonging to the healthcare institution." Meanwhile, Integrated Plan insurers are increasingly requiring doctors to sign contracts containing "Inspection and Right to Audit" clauses.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: These clauses grant insurers the right to inspect full medical records to verify claims.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The result is that doctors check NEHR for relevant history – past abortions, in-vitro fertilisation (IVF) treatment, mental health conditions, sexually transmitted infections – and note it in their files for clinical safety.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Because of these audit clauses, insurers then gain access to this sensitive, transcribed NEHR data, even if it is irrelevant to the current claim.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: A patient going in for gallbladder surgery may find their insurer reviewing their psychiatric history.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Section 17(1) provides that an individual may access and collect their own accessible health information.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The insurer's application form may include a new requirement: "Please attach a complete printout of your National Electronic Health Record." No printout, no policy.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Once the data leaves the system through legitimate patient access, it seems beyond the Bill's reach.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Even if insurers do not require a NEHR printout directly, they already have a right to refuse payouts if a pre-existing condition was not previously disclosed.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If an applicant fails to disclose a condition, one that now sits permanently in NEHR, the insurers can void the policy at claim time when they discover the non-disclosure through other means.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The existence of NEHR with its comprehensive longitudinal record makes non-disclosure almost impossible to sustain.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, I ask: one, does MOH agree that a transcription pathway where NEHR-derived information entering clinical notes and becomes accessible to insurers through audit clauses defeats the legislative intent of section 6?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Two, what if there is a data breach?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Four, will the Government review the inspection and right to audit clauses in Integrated Plan contracts to ensure that they did not circumvent the excluded purposes provisions?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: And five, if an insurer is found to utilise either pathway, what enforcement mechanisms will exist?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Will this be a matter for MAS, MOH or both?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Deputy Speaker, I now wish to speak to a broader question.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This Bill will create, for the first time, a comprehensive national database.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Social determinants, such as postal code, education, marital status; clinical outcomes, such as blood pressure readings over decades, medications prescribed; and soon, perhaps, genomic data from the SG100K project.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It is a "means of production"; not just of population health outcomes, but of significant economic value.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: So, how do we ensure that value from this national health data infrastructure, and its possible monetisation of any form, flows to citizens?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Globally, startups are experimenting with patient-centric data models, where individuals can choose to share their data for research and receive compensation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I believe a monopoly, such as Synapxe, may not experiment with such models.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Some players may try patient-centric approaches and the best models will emerge.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: To create the conditions for competition to discover it, that requires open APIs, interoperability standards like the opt-in mechanisms of the sort that my hon colleague Mr Fadli Fawzi mentioned, and a contestable application layer.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Section 8 provides that the Minister may designate a system operator to operate, administer and maintain the national electronic record system.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Synapxe, formerly known as IHiS, today employs about 3,500 people.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It serves as a technology backbone for our entire public healthcare system.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: When IHiS was set up in 2008, I believe the original vision was that it will operate on contestable principles.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: MOH will issue tenders, IHiS will compete, win some, lose some, it would have enough work to survive, but will need to compete elsewhere to thrive.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In doing so, it will face enough competition to stay efficient.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This model was the original plan for the Ministry of Defence and ST Engineering.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Dr Goh Keng Swee, speaking in 1977, said, "We do not own or run enterprises on ideological grounds.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: We expect Government-owned enterprises to be efficient, to make money and to expand whenever feasible.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If a Government-owned enterprise loses money, it is allowed to go bankrupt, and this has happened, fortunately, in very few instances." This was and is the discipline of contestability.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Government-owned enterprises were to be subject to market forces.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But the current model for Synapxe has drifted from this vision.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: An engineer is hired at $5,000 a month.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: That engineer's services are sold to public healthcare clusters at significantly higher rates.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If the mark-ups are excessive – and they can become excessive in the absence of competition – it can crowd out innovation and make the ecosystem weaker than it should be.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I believe a different model is possible and necessary.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It would return to the original contestable principles surrounding IHiS' creation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The first entity would be a core infrastructure company.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It would handle standard setting, data exchange protocols, security baselines and the NEHR plumbing.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This stays Government-owned and lean – perhaps a few hundred people.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It runs the pipes and sets the protocols but does not compete at the application layer.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The second entity would be a commercial services company.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It would handle system integration, consulting and vendor management.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This gets spun off – maybe privatised, maybe converted to a Government-linked company that must compete commercially, both domestically and internationally.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Second, MOH must reacquire the in-house capacity to be an intelligent buyer of technology services.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Without this capacity, the Ministry will find it hard to escape capture.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The goal is to ensure that the application layer – the layer where innovation happens – is open and contestable.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: I happen to think all this can be done within four to five years.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: This is the primary purpose and I support it fully; (b) a fair stake in data monetisation for every citizen.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If value is going to be extracted from the data, we should create conditions where citizens can likely share in it, not just bear the risk; and (c) an ecosystem catalyst for health-based startups.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: With open APIs and interoperability, Singapore can become a place for health tech innovation.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Startups can build on the NEHR platform, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) can compete for contracts.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The NEHR can become a flywheel for a more dynamic health tech ecosystem, one that benefits the Government, citizens and entrepreneurs alike, not merely a Government-only benefit and asset.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: It can improve care, reduce waste and enable the precision medicine of tomorrow.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: But a Bill that compels contribution must also come with robust ecosystem safeguards.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Those compelled to contribute must be protected from disproportionate burden or liability.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Since access controls do not exclude data from NEHR, a breach potentially exposes everything, regardless of restrictions.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: Today, insurers cannot access NEHR, but perhaps through transcription and audit clauses, they can access NEHR-derived information sitting in clinical notes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: In locking the front door, we must also lock the back door.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: If we are to build a national data asset, we must ensure that it is governed by contestable principles, not captured by a monopoly provider.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat (Aljunied)
text: The original vision for IHiS was discipline through competition.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: There are two aspects which I find essential for successful implementation that I wish to spotlight.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: First, there is to be comprehensive onboarding support for GPs, including innovative shared staffing arrangements for small clinics; and second, I would like to call for strengthened support for community partners to ensure seamless continuity of care across our healthcare ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: To achieve "One Patient, One Health Summary, One Care Journey", our GPs, particularly those operating small, independent practices, need adequate support to participate sustainably.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While most primary care clinics are already contributing to the NEHR, this figure masks significant challenges faced by small practitioners.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Stakeholder feedback had indicated that GP clinics and smaller healthcare organisations are worried about meeting cybersecurity and data security requirements as they have limited resources and administrative capacity.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is a valid concern as the burden falls on them to maintain cyber and data security.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: This is an ongoing challenge, even for well-resourced organisations globally.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unlike large hospital groups with dedicated IT departments and compliance teams, small GP clinics often operate with minimal administrative staff, tight margins and practitioners who are clinicians first, not IT specialists.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Hence, I would like to seek three clarifications from the Minister.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: It would be helpful for the GPs to have more details.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What is the maximum funding quantum per clinic?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Does it cover hardware, software, training and ongoing maintenance?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Will funding be provided upfront or reimbursed retrospectively?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Small practices operate on tight cash flow and cannot afford to frontload substantial IT investments without certainty of reimbursement.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Second, would MOH extend implementation support beyond technology to operational capacity?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: While NEHR-compatible systems address the technical dimension, the administrative burden of data entry, staff training and compliance monitoring remains substantial.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Small GP clinics often lack administrative staff dedicated solely to data management.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I propose that MOH explore small clinics jointly hiring and sharing data entry staff through collaborative arrangements or tapping on some form of shared resources.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Third, would MOH consider a calibrated enforcement framework that accounts for clinic size and capacity?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill appropriately provides that MOH work with healthcare providers to resolve non-compliance, such as technical challenges leading to non-contribution, before issuing formal directions or penalties.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: I hope that there could be special considerations given, for example, cases where it is a single-doctor clinic with two nurses should not be held to the same compliance timeline as a multi-site group practice with dedicated IT infrastructure.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The second aspect for a successful implementation calls for strengthened support for community partners to ensure seamless continuity of care across our healthcare ecosystem.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: We must ensure that data sharing between healthcare providers and community partners supports smooth continuity of care, particularly as patients transition from acute hospital settings to community care options.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Implementation requires operational readiness and active Ministry support for community partners.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would MOH share what technical and operational support will be provided to community partners?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Community care organisations – Active Ageing Centres, voluntary welfare organisations, befriending services – often lack the IT infrastructure and data governance expertise to receive, safely store and use health information securely.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would MOH extend support packages beyond healthcare providers to include community partners, funding secure data systems, staff training and compliance with data security requirements?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: (In Mandarin):   Would MOH share what technical and operational support will be provided to community partners?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Community care organisations – Active Ageing Centres, volunteer welfare organisations, befriending services – often lack the IT infrastructure and data governance expertise to receive, safely store and use health information securely.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Would MOH extend support packages beyond healthcare providers to include community partners, funding secure data systems, staff training and compliance with data security requirements?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The Bill currently limits data sharing to public sector entities – AIC, healthcare clusters and public agencies.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Over time, private community healthcare partners, nursing homes and home care providers should be included, subject to governance and data protection safeguards.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Equally, community partners need active Ministry support to fulfil their role in continuity of care.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: This vision of achieving nationwide contribution of health information into a central repository is a truly ambitious and challenging goal.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: But as with all things new, it has not come without its fair share of fear and trepidation from the ground.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: For years, our public sector healthcare institutions have been contributing to the NEHR.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: However, there are still private clinics and other healthcare establishments that have yet to modernise and digitise their patient records.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: And I agree with Members who have spoken so far that for those who struggle with new technology, it is particularly daunting to navigate the journey of digital transformation.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: In this respect, I know that Ministry officers have been making the necessary preparations for a long time.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: The draft guidelines have been made available, and I understand it will be published at such time when the HIB makes its successful passage through this House.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: To formulate these guidelines, there were numerous engagement sessions arranged by the Ministry involving various stakeholders, for example, the Academy of Medicine, the Singapore Medical Association and the Singapore Dental Association, as well as nurses, pharmacists and allied health professionals.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: As co-chair of the Workgroup, I was present at most, if not all, of these engagement sessions to hear and address the concerns from the ground and to obtain constructive feedback.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Some have mentioned that patients do not like to be asked repeatedly about their medical histories.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: But there is a need to emphasise that the primary source of health information remains with the patient.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: National health records can provide a back-up source of essential health data when patients are poor historians or are otherwise unable to provide information to their doctors, but it is not a replacement for the traditional way in which doctors interact with their patients through direct communication, which is so important if we are to build a strong doctor-patient partnership, one that is based on trust.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Integrated care also does not mean that we should expect doctors to routinely have to trawl through and read NEHR records before they even exchanged the first word with the patient.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We do need to ensure that the healthcare professionals who are users of the system see it as an asset, rather than a potential quagmire where missteps will engender swift punishment and legal liability.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: As for patients, they need to have trust in the National Health Records System and believe that it is there to serve their needs and safeguard their interests, and not at the expense of their privacy or autonomy.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Many concerns from the ground remain, for example, that time is needed for their practices to be compliance-ready, that they need technical support to deal with cybersecurity threats or simply to familiarise themselves with recommended practice guidelines and the statutory obligations that will be put in place once the Health Information Act comes into force.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: In addition, I would like to ask the Senior Minister of State if the Ministry intends to continue focusing on patient education efforts that will, in my view, be essential if we want patients to feel secure and have faith in how their sensitive health information will be handled.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: We are unlikely to gain all the benefits from this ambitious initiative if too many of our patients resort to setting controls on access due to fear or misconceptions.

speaker: Ms Kuah Boon Theng (Nominated Member)
text: Patient education, therefore, needs to continue to be a priority and we must continue to listen to and address their concerns and build their trust.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This Bill is not just about technology or compliance.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is about trust – trust between patients and providers, between Government and citizens, and between institutions and the professionals who serve in them.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: It is essential for our transition from hospital-centric care to community-based care, particularly as we confront the twin challenges of an ageing population and the rising burden of chronic disease.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Today, I would like to focus on these four areas: one, supporting community healthcare practitioners and GPs in onboarding to the NEHR system; two, improving data transition between Government hospitals and the community sector; three, strengthening support for allied health professionals (AHPs); and four, addressing patients' concerns about data protection thresholds and breach safeguards.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The vision of "One Patient, One Health Record, One Care Journey" is compelling.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But to realise it, we must ensure that practitioners outside hospital settings, especially GPs in smaller, independent practices, have adequate support to participate meaningfully.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Today, most primary care clinics already contribute to NEHR.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is driven by Healthier SG's integration requirements.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Many GPs operate with lean teams, limited administrative bandwidth and modest technical capacity.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For them, NEHR integration can feel like a burden, even if its clinical value is clear.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But for some GPs and smaller practices, this may still be a tight timeline for them.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: I urge MOH to adopt a calibrated enforcement approach, working collaboratively with GPs to resolve technical challenges rather than defaulting to penalties.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is crucial for building a genuine partnership with community practitioners.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Bill rightly seeks to enable seamless data transition between Government hospitals and community healthcare partners.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This is vital for the continuity of care as patients move from acute to community settings.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: However, we must ensure that the data transition process is not merely technically compliant, but genuinely supportive of community-based practitioners.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: When a patient is discharged from a Government hospital, the community GP or AHP taking over care should receive comprehensive, timely, clinically relevant information.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: This would extend data sharing arrangements beyond public institutions, strengthening care continuity across the entire healthcare ecosystem.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: AHPs – physiotherapists, radiographers, occupational therapists, speech and language therapists and radiation therapists – play indispensable roles in patient care and should have access to relevant NEHR information.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: In particular, AHPs are crucial in managing chronic conditions, rehabilitation and preventive care in the community and outpatient settings.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: They need access to medication histories, adverse drug reactions, recent investigations and relevant diagnoses to deliver safe and effective care.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: For them, access to relevant NEHR information is not optional.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Yet, the stakeholder feedback indicates concerns about whether all AHPs will have equal access rights and whether sufficient safeguards exist to ensure they access only clinically relevant information for their specific roles.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The Bill provides role-based access controls, ensuring AHPs can only access data relevant to their duties.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, establish clear practice guidelines for each AHP profession, specifying what NEHR data is relevant and when access is clinically justified.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Second, ensure that AHP associations are active partners in training and upskilling of their members on NEHR use, medico-legal responsibilities and safeguards.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The MOH will publish guidelines on appropriate use of NEHR to address medico-legal concerns, but professional bodies should help manage implementation through their own continuing education programmes.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we want integrated care, we must empower every professional who contributes to it.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Patients must feel confident that their most sensitive information is safeguarded.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Healthcare providers must report data breaches to MOH and affected individuals if the breaches result in significant harm.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: But what of smaller breaches, affecting 50, 100 or 200 people?

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: First, all breaches, regardless of scale, must be assessed and remedied.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: The MOH's enforcement will take seriously even breaches affecting small numbers of people.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Two, patients should be notified of significant breaches affecting any number of individuals.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Three, repeated smaller breaches that reveal systemic vulnerabilities must trigger decisive corrective action.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Four, patients should be able to view access logs for their records and flag suspicious activity to MOH.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: Citizen monitoring can be a powerful supplement to regulatory oversight.

speaker: Dr Choo Pei Ling (Chua Chu Kang)
text: If we succeed, this Bill will not only strengthen our healthcare system but also deepen the confidence of Singaporeans in it.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Growing up in the heartland and now serving in public healthcare, I have lived and worked among Singaporeans across generations, across every walk of life.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Every day, I sit across the table from patients: the uncle in his 60s managing six chronic conditions; the young mother bringing her newborn for a jaundice review, hoping the hospital's records have already reached me; the elderly auntie who cannot remember which medicines to take; and the caregivers, trying to make sense of it all for loved ones who cannot.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: They come because they trust we will help them make sense of a system that can feel overwhelming.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: And I work alongside nurses, care coordinators, allied health staff, administrators and fellow doctors.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: People who entered healthcare to help, doing their best under difficult conditions.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I speak today for both: for patients and families who depend on the system and for healthcare workers who make it work.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: One patient, one health summary, one care journey.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Patients must trust that their health information will not be used against them.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But the Bill is only as good as the trust it builds, from patients and from providers.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: First, the boundaries are clear, the grey zone is not.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The Bill tells us what we must not do, but not what we must do, or how much is enough.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I take a history, examine her and I am satisfied.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Three months later, it turns out she had early lung cancer.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: A CT scan done elsewhere six months ago showed a lung nodule.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: If I click "Result A" but not the adjacent "Result B" because it seems unrelated to the current consult, is that reasonable?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Or will I be asked, later, why I did not check?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Clause 99 protects those who act in good faith and with reasonable care, but it does not define what reasonable care looks like.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: In practice, clinicians exercise professional judgement every day.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But what does reasonable care and professional judgement look like with 10 minutes of consultation time and 10 years of records?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I am not asking for immunity from accountability.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: How we should document the choices we make, against the ever-increasing complexity and demands of clinical care.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Not a one-time circular, but updated as systems and practice evolve.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Next, governance is central, enablement must be central too.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Standards are set by the Ministry, but implementation is local and the burden falls unevenly.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Public institutions have the resources to maintain systems, keep them updated and respond when things go wrong.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: We cannot say the same for private practice.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I still speak to friends from medical school, former colleagues now in private practice.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: The solo GP in Bedok, the small group practice in Jurong: they face the same data security and breach reporting standards under Parts 4 and 5, with far fewer resources.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I know senior doctors, still sharp, still caring, who are thinking of hanging up their white coats early.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Not because they cannot practise medicine, but because they cannot keep up with the infrastructural demands.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Clinicians should be caring for patients, not managing systems.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Patient data must be protected, but enablement must match governance.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Central standards require central support and this support must be sustained, not just during roll-out.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: This could take many forms: shared IT services, pooled cybersecurity monitoring, simplified compliance pathways.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Existing structures like Primary Care Networks could be leveraged.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: These need not be free, but they must be accessible and sustained; not tapering off after implementation, but continuing for as long as the obligations continue.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Part 7 provides for portability of health information.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Healthier SG encourages patients to build long-term relationships with one family doctor.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Trust takes time and NEHR supports this, giving access to specialist and hospital records, enabling coordinated care.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Yet, seamless portability makes it easier to move between private providers.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: If records follow effortlessly, why stay with one doctor?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: There are valid reasons to change primary providers: relocation, a breakdown in relationship perhaps.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: But if portability inadvertently undermines continuity, NEHR risks enabling fragmentation.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Episodic care from whichever provider is nearest, cheapest or most convenient, leading to wasted resources.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: I ask the Minister: what measures will ensure that portability reinforces, rather than weakens, the care relationships Healthier SG seeks to build?

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It matters to the patient hoping the next doctor knows what the last one did.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It matters to the clinician wanting to do the right thing but uncertain of the rules.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: It matters to the small practice owner worried about compliance.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: Trust is built through clarity, through support, through coherence between policies meant to work together.

speaker: Dr Haresh Singaraju (Nominated Member)
text: While I support this Bill, I urge the Minister to address these concerns, please.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: You see, as care becomes more complex, with more providers, more settings and more chronic conditions, patients often carry their own medical history across the system.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For many Singaporeans, the most stressful part of a health episode is not just the illness alone, but it is the friction that comes along with it.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They have to repeat their story with every medical visit.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They struggle to recall the medication names – sometimes I do – past dosages, or test results that sit in different institutions.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For those caring for ageing parents, they become our human bridge as they juggle between appointment letters, WhatsApp photos of prescriptions and fragmented notes of different providers.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Therefore, having a well-governed national health record reduces this burden.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It supports safer handover between stakeholders in the healthcare systems, such as our GPs, specialists, hospitals and community partners.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It also lowers the risk of missed allergies, drug interactions and also unnecessary repeated tests that cost time, money and anxiety.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This Bill puts the NEHR system on a clearer legal footing, including governance of access, use and safeguards.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For these reasons, I support the intent and direction of this Bill.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: That said, Mr Speaker, I would like to raise three broad points which I hope will be used to strengthen trust and confidence in implementation.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: My first point pertains to individual regarding sensitive health data and access restrictions.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Sharing information about a cough, a vaccination, a fracture, is usually straightforward.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: But many Singaporeans will understandably feel unease when information relates to areas where stigma still exists, such as mental health conditions, sexually transmitted diseases, HIV status, substance abuse, self-harm or records that may expose abuse.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The fear is not only about embarrassment, but it is about the consequences that will come along too.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Specifically, how would such information affect their employability.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: This is why the Bill's safeguards matters, because access is purpose-limited, it is role-based, logged, restrictions are auditable and misuse attracts serious consequences.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: It gives individuals the ability to impose access restrictions.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The ability to impose access restrictions provides individuals with the peace of mind.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In essence, it gives that reassurance to say that, "Hey, I can see my records.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: I can understand my records, and if I wish, I can limit the information the other party can see", which is important because this is how we build trust.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: The message should remain consistent and prominent as the Bill is being implemented.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And against this backdrop, I have two clarifications on this.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As we have seen in the recent Community Development Council (CDC) January vouchers, where even after multiple rounds of education, some seniors still do not feel confident in claiming their vouchers digitally.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They still come to our Community Centres to collect hardcopy vouchers.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Against this backdrop, I wonder what assisted pathways will be available for residents who wish to understand and also know how they can manage their access restrictions?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Could this include in-person support at polyclinics, hospitals or even trusted community touchpoints, so that the right to impose, to understand access restrictions, it is not only for those who are digitally confident, but for every single Singaporean?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Second, I wonder, will citizens also be able to view their access history in a way that is simple and meaningful; and will MOH also clearly explain what the access history does and does not capture?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: For example, a resident showed me that if you go to our HealthHub's FAQ page, it says: "Your healthcare professionals may be accessing your records from their own Electronic Medical Records (EMR) systems.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: And what this means is that it would not be captured in the access history, because they are looking for information through their own system.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If we want to build trust, then we must be clear what the access history can capture and cannot capture.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Beyond these two questions, that got me thinking about the issue of data completeness.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: As clinicians document care in their own clinic and hospital systems, the NEHR depends on what is contributed through integration.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Other systems abroad also show that governance alone is not enough.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Some jurisdictions mandate provider contributions through law, while others rely on technical readiness or voluntary participation.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Regardless, the NEHR will only reach its fullest potential if data contributions are consistent and timely.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: We need to ensure that this contribution is consistent, prompt, with good quality, across providers.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Would there be positive levers such as integration support, performance feedback, recognition of good practices and contributors to be considered for the rest to learn from.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Smaller clinics and some community providers may need more time and practical support to meet new requirements properly.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In practical terms, what this could look like means standard templates, shared tools, training resources, a clear helpdesk and escalation pathway and where necessary, support to uplift baseline cyber security since the system is only as strong as its weakest link.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In these interactions, a Singaporean shared with me, and I also understand so, because I have experienced that through my friends who are young parents as well.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They shared that some of them would prefer to go overseas for screenings or procedures, because they perceive it to be cheaper and/or faster.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: In particular, would the Ministry consider capturing reliable and credible health information data from abroad in our system?

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Because in my experience when I spoke with some parents, when they have newly-born, they are quite excited to search for and know the gender of the child.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: They would go overseas to do a quick test so that they will know whether it is a boy or a girl.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: Of course, this should be considered with the intent that any integration of overseas health information should be done to strengthen our continuity of care and not compromise data quality and clinical safety.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: If implemented with clear communication, assisted access pathways, and credible transparency, this Bill can help Singapore build a health data ecosystem that is both enabling and trusted.

speaker: Mr David Hoe (Jurong East-Bukit Batok)
text: With this point, Mr Speaker, I support the Bill.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Before that, I declare my interest as an orthopaedic surgeon currently in private practice.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Drawing from both my clinical experience and ground feedback that I have gathered, I will focus my remarks on two areas that have surfaced repeatedly: one, the practical realities faced by clinicians, particularly in smaller healthcare settings; and two, the importance of patient trust, supported by robust access and privacy safeguards.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: At the same time, many doctors, particularly those in smaller GP practices, specialist clinics and dental clinics, have raised practical questions about how this Bill affects their medico-legal responsibilities.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I think this was alluded to earlier by Dr Haresh as well.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: First, I would like to seek clarification from the Minister on the intended role of the NEHR in daily clinical practice.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Good medicine still begins with history-taking, physical examination, and the doctor's professional judgment, based on the presentation of the patient at that material point in time.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Digital tools should enhance clinical decision-making, not replace it.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Clear articulation of this principle will help address concerns that clinicians could be exposed to liability simply for not accessing NEHR in every encounter.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As clinicians are required to contribute to and access NEHR responsibly, clear, practical guidelines on appropriate use will help healthcare professionals act with confidence: firstly, knowing when access is appropriate; next, how to document decisions made on the access of NEHR data; and then, how to meet their obligations without fear of inadvertent non-compliance.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I therefore welcome the Ministry's intention to provide guidance and training to all healthcare professionals.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Third, I wish to speak for smaller providers who are concerned about cybersecurity and data protection requirements.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Unlike large institutions, many smaller clinics operate with limited manpower and resources, as already alluded to by previous speakers.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In this regard, I do welcome the funding support and the use of whitelisted systems to help smaller providers comply safely and securely.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: A calibrated enforcement posture, coupled with practical assistance, will be key to ensuring that compliance strengthens care rather than becoming an administrative burden.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Ultimately, Mr Speaker, clinicians want to do the right thing for their patients and for the healthcare system.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This Bill works best when it enables clinicians, rather than paralyse them.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Patients share deeply personal information because they trust it will be used solely for their care and not to disadvantage them in any way.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Unfortunately, on the ground, I personally have seen instances that undermine this trust.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: There have been cases where insurers have written to multiple clinics in the vicinity of a patient's residence, seeking information about the patient's medical history in the context of an insurance claim.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These broad and often non-specific requests are deeply troubling because they go back in years.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: They ask about someone presenting with a particular symptom, 10 to 15 years before the current claim is being made.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This places our clinicians in a very difficult position and risk compromising confidentiality between providers who may actually have no direct care relationship with the patient.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These practices underscore why clear legal boundaries around access and use of health information are essential.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: In this regard, I strongly support the safeguards embedded in this Bill.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I understand that access to the NEHR will be both role based and purpose specific.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: Healthcare professionals may only access records for patients under their own care and only for direct patient care purposes.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This clarity sends a strong and necessary signal and directly addresses public concerns about misuse.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I also welcome the transparency features enabled through HealthHub.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: These features reinforce accountability and uphold public confidence.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This ensures that patient autonomy does not inadvertently compromise patient safety.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I was glad to hear fellow Member Mr Fadli prioritise patient autonomy in his speech earlier.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: This is why I believe a restricted access approach, rather than a complete opt-out approach would be more beneficial to patients, clearly demonstrating that in medical emergencies in the case of an opt-out system, critical information more not be available to the attending physicians.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
