text: This includes inmates under the care of the Singapore Prison Service.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: As we aspire to have inmates eventually transition back into the community or require care in our public healthcare institutions, timely access to critical medical information can be important for their safety and continuity of care.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: I seek the Minister's clarification on how such health information is treated within the broader framework of the NEHR and how safeguards are applied in these contexts.

speaker: Dr Hamid Razak (West Coast-Jurong West)
text: When trust is preserved, seamless care becomes possible.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: I suspend the Sitting and will take the Chair at 7.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Sitting accordingly suspended  at 7.13 pm until 7.25 pm.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Members have raised a number of thoughtful views and constructive comments which I will address in four broad themes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But before I do that, I would like to address the points made by the Member Mr Kenneth Tiong around the organisation of and his views on Synapxe, the health tech agency that implements many of the IT projects in MOH.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As that topic does not pertain to the specifics of the HIB, I encourage Mr Tiong to raise a separate Parliamentary Question or raise the issue separately from today's debate.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But suffice to say that Synapxe is not a commercial entity.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Its fundamental role is to support MOH in delivering digital health and IT services to benefit the healthcare clusters to deliver better healthcare services to our Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: There are four broad themes of comments that came in.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: First, it is around the safeguards for patients.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Second, the obligations and support measures for healthcare providers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And fourthly, the sharing of non-NEHR health information.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Yip Hon Weng, Mr David Hoe, Dr Wan Rizal, Dr Hamid Razak and Mr Fadili Fawzi highlighted the importance of safeguarding access to and the use of patients' NEHR information.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And this has been a focus for us when we carried out the public consultation and prepared this Bill.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: There are broadly two sets of concerns that we hear from individuals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The first is how a patient's NEHR information will be adequately safeguarded and accessed only as needed by healthcare professionals and providers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Of special concern is the access to health information that may be deemed more sensitive.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: There were also related questions about the Access Restriction feature.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, that is the first set of concerns.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The second is around whether their NEHR information would be used beyond healthcare, such as for employment and insurance purposes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have been operating the NEHR for 15 years.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Importantly, the vast majority of healthcare providers are already onboard – all public healthcare institutions, most private hospitals and the bulk of the GP clinics.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, this is a system that has been operating for many years.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And we have built in various ex-ante safeguards into the design of the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This includes role-based access, such that authorised healthcare professionals can only access the types of health information required for their specific patient care roles.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We also have technical controls and regular ex-post audits to flag unauthorised accesses to the NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Healthcare professionals who access NEHR in an unauthorised manner could also be referred to the relevant Professional Boards or Councils for further action.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Dennis Tan spoke about offences and whether the $1 million maximum fine was sufficient.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The breaches to the HIB are serious and we take this seriously.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, a conviction involves not just fines, it is imprisonment as well.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But more basically, we take an approach that is more supportive, working together with our healthcare providers, the healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These are people – nurses, clinicians and administrators, who want to do well, who want to serve the patients, who want to take care of the patients.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And we want to take a supportive role and approach to uplift data security and cybersecurity postures, not a punitive approach.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Alex Yeo asked about audits on unauthorised accesses of the NEHR and Mr Tiong asked if Synapxe would proactively monitor against unauthorised access.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Synapxe, the NEHR system operator, conducts regular audits and ongoing monitoring to detect suspicious behaviour or atypical patterns, including in response to patient alerts.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, accessing the NEHR information of a patient who has not recently visited any healthcare provider is a flag.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Synapxe will conduct investigations to determine whether an unauthorised access has occurred.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Synapxe will regularly review its audit plans, including frequency, best practices and the use of new tools like artificial intelligence to ensure that the regime is robust.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Patients can monitor which healthcare providers have accessed their NEHR information and flag any unauthorised access to the authorities for investigation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The logs will show access at the healthcare institution level to keep the function simple, useable and practical.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In a multi-disciplinary team, healthcare professionals across different roles may access the patient's NEHR information at different times of the patient's care journey.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Depending on the patient's condition, it is also not uncommon for nurses, pharmacists or allied health professionals to need access.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In our healthcare system, the institution is ultimately responsible for care to its patient.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: HealthHub access logs will show all accesses to NEHR, regardless of whether the access is through EMR or the portal.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, just to clarify on his point earlier.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Louis Chua, Mr Yip, Dr Hamid, Mr Hoe and Mr Tiong have commented on the need for safeguards for such information.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Such health information includes sexually transmitted infections, delusional disorders and schizophrenia.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The diagnoses and test results that confirm the condition are subject to additional safeguards.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: First, there are restrictions on who can access this information.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Only a select group of healthcare professionals are allowed to access this information, based on their role in caring for the patient diagnosed with the health condition.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, a nurse who is working in a psychiatric ward will have access to the psychiatric condition of the patient he or she is caring for.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Second, before an authorised healthcare professional can access these types of health information, they will be subject to a double log-in, which requires the authorised healthcare professional to re-verify their credentials before access.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This ensures that such information is only accessed when needed and avoids accidental access.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Accesses to such health information are more closely audited by Synapxe and cases of unauthorised access to NEHR information will be investigated and penalties imposed.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As I mentioned earlier in my opening speech, we do not encourage this, as it could lead to adverse impact on care delivery for the patient.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To address the queries raised by Members, the Access Restrictions have been designed to balance the impact to patient care; considering the welfare and interest of the patient, while taking into consideration their concerns around privacy.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, patients may restrict access to their NEHR information at the healthcare institution level, but not at an individual healthcare professional level.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As I have mentioned earlier, care delivery is team-based and increasingly multi-disciplinary.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is not operationally feasible to restrict access to specific healthcare professionals but not others, when they all work in a team, in the same healthcare institution.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is aligned with good practices we observed elsewhere, like in Australia.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Health information will be contributed to NEHR even if Access Restrictions are in place.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As pointed out by Dr Hamid, who brings in a practitioner's perspective, an incomplete record, including if individuals opt not to contribute select healthcare information deemed to be more sensitive, will significantly reduce the utility of NEHR in supporting healthcare professionals to provide quality care and could pose a safety risk.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In certain situations, access to such records in a timely manner could save lives, as I mentioned earlier in my opening speech.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: One example would be when a doctor or pharmacist needs to have the ability to access drug interactions and his job is hindered due to incomplete medication information, the patient could suffer unintended consequences, especially in emergency situations when the patient may not be able to respond.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It also ensures that if patients change their mind in future, for instance, when they are older and remove such Access Restrictions, there would be no gap in NEHR information and this was a valuable learning point when MOH colleagues engaged other jurisdictions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The approach we are adopting aims to achieve a balance between patient choice and ensuring that patients receive better and more coordinated patient care.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Next, I would like to also thank Members like Mr Yip, Mr Hoe, Mr Chua, Mr Fadli and Ms Kuah Boon Theng for highlighting the importance of educating the public on the implications of placing Access Restrictions and supporting patients who are less digitally savvy.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MOH will work with the healthcare institutions to set-up physical touchpoints for those who require help with placing Access Restrictions and help them understand the implications of doing so.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Alternatively, patients may seek the help of trusted individuals, like their family members and caregivers to place Access Restrictions on their behalf.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Yip raised the concern that the act of placing an Access Restriction may itself become a source of stigma or adverse inference.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This Access Restriction will be known only to the healthcare providers managing the patient and all healthcare professionals are bound by their respective professional bodies' ethical codes and ethical guidelines to treat all patients fairly and without prejudice.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We understand Singaporeans' concerns about the potential discrimination or stigmatisation they may face if their health information is revealed to their employer or insurer.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: On this, I would like to reiterate three points that I have made earlier in my opening speech.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Second, healthcare professionals are also prohibited from accessing NEHR for employment or insurance purposes, except for prescribed statutory medical examinations, which I will talk on later, or where authorised by other written law or Order of the Court.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Third, the HIB imposes strict penalties for any unauthorised access to NEHR, with higher penalties for prohibited employment or insurance purposes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Dr Wan Rizal asked whether statutory medical examinations may provide a backdoor for employers to gain access to NEHR information.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have no plans to expand this list to include employment-related screenings that are not necessary to protect the public and the individual.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The current practice for employment-related screenings will remain – where doctors rely on their history-taking, clinical assessment and their own existing medical records for the individual, if any, without access to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: On Mr Yeo's query, on whether MOH would consider allowing individuals to give consent for their NEHR information to be accessed for insurance purposes for some situations, I would like to reiterate that NEHR is primarily for patient care purposes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: When insurers request for health information, the current practice is for healthcare providers and professionals to rely on their medical records and patient interactions, which include history-taking, as well as physical examinations, to prepare the necessary reports for the insurer.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This will continue to be the case after the HIB is enacted.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To Mr Tiong's query, healthcare providers and professionals should prepare separate medical reports, memos or clinical summaries for the insurer, instead of providing their raw medical records, such as printouts from their clinical medical records.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is because raw medical records contain extensive information, including potentially irrelevant information.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Where NEHR information is referred to during a medical examination, information relevant to the episode would be validated or confirmed with the patient during history taking and may be captured in the provider's own medical records, together with the doctor's clinical assessment.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Such information would then be treated as part of the provider's own medical records.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Healthcare providers and professionals will need to carefully assess what information in their own medical records is relevant and necessary to include in the report provided to an insurer.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MOH has issued a circular to healthcare providers and a guidance note to insurers to clearly state these positions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Healthcare providers may inform MOH if there are any inappropriate requests for NEHR information for insurance purposes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Dr Haresh asked if mandatory contributions, coupled with access will encourage episodic care affecting initiatives, such as Healthier SG, which encourages building a trusted relationship between patients and their family doctors.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Hoe asked about the requirement to contribute information in a timely and accurate manner and the treatment of overseas medical records.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Fadli Fawzi asked about the level of details of key health information to be contributed to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Bill requires healthcare providers to contribute accurate and complete health information in a timely manner.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This ultimately benefits patients by enabling their healthcare providers to access all relevant health information to provide the best care.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Take a Healthier SG family doctor as an example.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The bill will allow the doctor to deliver better patient care, taking account of the patient's medical history across different settings, including private specialist clinics.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This enables the doctor to build a trusted, and hopefully lifelong relationship towards better health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And to help healthcare providers comply with the contribution requirements in the Bill, we have whitelisted health information management systems (HIMS) that have the requisite technical features and encourage all healthcare providers to subscribe to these HIMS.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Nevertheless, patients can bring their overseas health records to their local healthcare providers, who may then incorporate relevant information into their own medical records and once incorporated, these records will be contributed to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To Mr Fadli's query, NEHR is designed to be a "One Health Summary".

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will only require the contribution of health information prescribed in the First Schedule of the Bill and not the doctor's detailed clinical notes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The design of the system and the data pipes take in only the prescribed data types.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, if a patient has diabetes and is prescribed with insulin, the doctor will only contribute "diabetes" as a diagnosis and "insulin" as the medication.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, only information that is needed for continuity of care.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: However, I would like to reiterate that the primary purpose of the NEHR is to support and enhance the continuity of care for patients.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Hence, the HIB provides for NEHR access for licensed healthcare institutions.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Within these institutions, NEHR access is only provided for healthcare professionals with clinical or care planning roles.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is the core principle governing NEHR access.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: However, we recognise that as care models develop and evolve, we may need to grant new providers or services access to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In doing so, we will consider factors such as whether NEHR information is required for that role and whether the provider or service is able to comply with the HIB's requirements.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Prior to changing the scope of providers that may access NEHR, we will consult relevant stakeholders and publicly communicate the changes through the MOH website.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: NEHR was set up to facilitate patient care and the information within NEHR is primarily intended to be shared across healthcare providers for that purpose.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is a consistent principle adopted by other jurisdictions that we have studied.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MOH is of the view that identifiable health information should generally be interpreted and managed by qualified healthcare professionals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Therefore, when parties seek MOH's views on this, MOH will suggest that such parties consider alternative data sources or ways of achieving its policy intent instead of using NEHR information or involve qualified healthcare professionals to partner parties in meeting the intent.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For public health purposes under the HIB, NEHR information may be needed in certain situations, for example, to quickly identify and enable healthcare providers to contact affected patients in the event of a major drug contamination incident.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Another example is in the event of an outbreak of a serious infectious disease, there may not be sufficient time nor would it be feasible to seek consent from individuals to use their NEHR information to contain the outbreak.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: De-identified NEHR information may also be needed for public policy analysis and planning purposes, such as to review healthcare utilisation trends or to analyse the cost effectiveness of medicines.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I have given some examples to the queries raised by Members on the scenarios in which those clauses apply.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As a general rule, MOH will ensure requests for NEHR information have sound basis before supporting it.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For all supported requests, whether from private entities such as academic institutions and health-related organisations or from public agencies under other written laws, MOH will share only the necessary data required to fulfil the intent.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: For example, for requests from the Police to locate missing persons, we only provide administrative information about visits to healthcare providers without details of the patient's medical condition.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This enables the Police to confirm if missing persons have been warded in an emergency and in turn alert worried family members.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Requesting parties will also be required to protect the data against loss and against unauthorised access, use, modification, disclosure or other misuse.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Chua and Mr Fadli asked specifically about the use of NEHR for research.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: De-identified NEHR health information may be shared through established platforms such as TRUST under the National Research Foundation for research purposes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This could include training for artificial intelligence models.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Where requests are received from commercial parties, possibly for commercial purposes, we are extremely cautious in assessing such requests, including whether the sharing of such data is helpful in contributing to better healthcare and better health outcomes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: A number of Members, including Mr Yip and Mr Dennis Tan asked about the resilience and security standards for NEHR, particularly in light of the SingHealth data breach in 2018.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And NEHR is complying with the relevant resilience and security requirements for Government systems recommended by this committee.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I must add that, really, the lesson from the SingHealth data breach is that we were open and transparent about the issue, convened a Committee of Inquiry, learned our lessons, applied them and made sure we work very hard to prevent such breaches from recurring.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We took those lessons to heart as we built up our cybersecurity and data security standards.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Additionally, there are several lines of defence before the NEHR database, with intrusion detection at various parts of the network.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Timely hardware, software and application upgrades are implemented, which include security patches as well as security controls to detect and block suspicious traffic from external sources.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MOH and Synapxe will continue to work with the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore, GovTech and independent auditing firms to conduct regular cybersecurity reviews and security assessments.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I would also like to thank Mr Yip for his feedback on the need to make NEHR more user-friendly.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I assure him we will continue to invest in the improvement of NEHR's technology and features to help healthcare providers quickly identify the most relevant information for their patients.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Relatedly, Mr Yip, Dr Choo, Mr Hoe, Ms Joan Pereira and a number of Members like Mr Fadli Fawzi, Mr Tiong and Mr Dennis Tan asked for further details on the cybersecurity and incident management requirements, including their feasibility and the availability of MOH support.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This is an existing requirement in laws such as the Personal Data Protection Act and Healthcare Services Act 2020.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The Bill's cybersecurity and data security requirements are based on these existing standards and legal requirements, but contextualised for the healthcare sector.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These include frameworks such as the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore's Cyber Essentials Mark and the Infocomm Media Development Authority's Data Protection Essentials, which were designed to be accessible and implementable by smaller organisations.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Examples of these requirements include the use of anti-malware solutions and firewalls in computers, the backing up of essential business information and data storage practices.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Healthcare providers will also need to train their staff on cyber-hygiene and data governance practices to ensure safe and secure access to health information.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: On the incident management framework, healthcare providers and their HIMS providers must put in place a framework to identify, resolve and mitigate cybersecurity and data breaches.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: This includes notifying MOH of prescribed security incidents and implementing mechanisms and processes to detect and respond to incidents such as ransomware attacks or unauthorised access to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But even with the best preventive measures, a data breach may still occur.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Once notified, MOH will work with the healthcare providers to understand the root cause of the breach, the extent of the data exposed, the potential harm to patients, and the containment and mitigation measures that need to be implemented.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In the event of any data breach, healthcare providers are expected to take necessary measures to remediate the situation and prevent such incidents from occurring again.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Where MOH is of the view that the mitigation or preventive measures are inadequate, we will work with the healthcare providers on implementing the appropriate measures.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Additionally, MOH will only require significant breaches to be notified in alignment with the approach under existing legal frameworks such as the PDPA.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These details will be set out in subsidiary legislation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I appreciate the concerns that Members have raised about the support needed for smaller providers, especially smaller GP clinics.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I mentioned earlier that with Healthier SG, most GP clinics have already onboarded to NEHR, with the support of MOH.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MOH recognises the importance of providing healthcare providers with reasonable time to comply with the HIB requirements and will offer the necessary support for healthcare providers to prepare and adapt their systems and processes.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We see them as a valuable partner in supporting the continuity of care in the community.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: There are also other support packages to engage professional services from whitelisted service providers to implement cyber and data security requirements.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Additionally, resources, guidance materials and training programmes will be available to help healthcare providers, including our community health partners, to meet the HIB cybersecurity and data protection requirements on an ongoing basis.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We would like to reassure providers that with this support in place, healthcare providers will be better enabled and supported to implement the relevant requirements.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We acknowledge the concerns raised by Mr Yip about potential fear-mongering tactics by some vendors.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To address this, MOH is developing basic service packages specifically tailored to the needs of solo practitioners and small and medium enterprises so that they can self-help and prevent overselling of unnecessary services.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are also establishing clear guidelines for whitelisted service providers on appropriate engagement practices and transparent pricing.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Healthcare providers that encounter unethical practices by whitelisted service providers can report them to MOH.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Additionally, we recognise that there is a small group of what Members call the pen-and-paper clinics that may face challenges in digitalising their clinics and meeting the Bill's requirements.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: As Members highlighted, these clinics may require additional implementation support.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is critical for clinical documentation, transmission of information between providers and laboratories, and supports timely coordination with other providers.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Today, most clinics already have some form of IT system for clinic management, accounting and billing.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Going forward, digital tools will increasingly become important, enabling clinics to rely on clinical decision support systems to close care gaps and deliver safer care.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Therefore, in recent years, we have strengthened the digitalisation in the private primary care sector to support Healthier SG and other national initiatives.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Across the GP sector, more than 80% of them are on Clinic Management Systems.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, there are a large number of clinics, a vast number of them, already embarking on the digitalisation efforts.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And we are supporting the remaining clinics to digitalise and onboard suitable systems to enable better delivery of care.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: To Ms Joan Pereira's query if smaller clinics could collaborate on shared resources, this is a good idea for smaller clinics to explore.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: PCNs not only provide peer leadership and support to small or solo GP practices, they also offer administrative assistance through the PCN headquarters.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The PCNs will continue to offer advice and support to member clinics, share resources to smoothen the clinics' journey in digitalisation and fulfilling NEHR contribution.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will further consider Mr Dennis Tan's and Ms Pereira's suggestions on shared IT support services as part of the roll-out.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And this is why we encourage all healthcare providers to adopt a whitelisted HIMS, which automates the process of contributing relevant health information to NEHR.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: That said, for smaller clinics that may require more time to digitalise, we will make available an alternative contribution channel so that these clinics will be able to start contributing data when required, while MOH continues to work with them on their digitalisation plans.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ms Kuah reflected concerns from the ground about time and effort needed for compliance, and if MOH will take these considerations in event of non-compliance, especially in the initial period.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: MOH has worked closely with healthcare providers and professionals and have been engaging them over the last few years.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Second, to support their transition, guidance materials and dedicated support channels will be made available from the second quarter of this year to help providers and professionals understand their options and navigate the process.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Third, should there be challenges complying with the Bill by the required timelines, MOH will consider the facts of each case carefully and assist where appropriate.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Dr Hamid Razak and Dr Choo Pei Ling enquired about how MOH intends to support healthcare professionals, noting that they have concerns about increased liability arising from the HIB.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I think Dr Haresh also pointed out concerns from healthcare professionals on medical and legal liabilities and how they should think about it.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We have been engaging the professional bodies and speaking to them over a period of time, and have taken their suggestions, ideas and feedback on board.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These guidelines will apply not only to doctors but also to other healthcare professionals accessing NEHR, such as dentists, nurses and allied health professionals.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Accessing patients' NEHR information is not compulsory under the HIB.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: NEHR supports and complements existing clinical practices, including good history-taking and physical examinations.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The HIB does not change existing standards and practices.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Healthcare professionals are encouraged to consider a range of factors before deciding whether NEHR access is required for a particular consultation, such as whether more information is required based on the information gleaned from the history-taking and physical examinations or whether health records in NEHR would be relevant to the particular consultation.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will also support professional bodies in ensuring their members' compliance with the Bill.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Ms Pereira enquired about the timeline for enabling community health partners' sharing of such health information to be covered under the HIB.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Mr Louis Chua asked why the HIB enables the sharing of non-NEHR health information without consent.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Today, AIC shares data with community partners to enable them to engage and provide befriending services or care to seniors.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: However, on the ground, there are difficulties with obtaining consent for data-sharing.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Referencing my earlier example of Mr Lim, the 72-year-old gentlemen who is managing his diabetes condition.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: He stopped visiting his local polyclinic and his polyclinic has faced difficulties in contacting him to obtain consent.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: The HIB will address this by providing an additional channel for the sharing of health information.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: AIC can then prioritise engaging Mr Lim to check on his well-being and link him with the necessary support as needed.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: On whether to include other community health partners, like Active Ageing Centres and use cases in the future, MOH will carefully assess whether these other entities and use cases facilitate quality care and care continuity for patients.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will consider their readiness to meet the various responsibilities that come with sharing health information, such as cybersecurity and data security requirements under the Bill and we will consult key stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Senior Minister of State Tan, if I could just ask you to hold on for a minute, because you have reached your time limit.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Any community health partners which are added will be publicly communicated, including through MOH's website.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We will work with and support healthcare providers and healthcare professionals in achieving this goal.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Through our collective efforts, Singaporeans can benefit from better coordinated care, enhanced quality of care and lower costs.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Are there clarifications for Senior Minister of State Tan?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: I also thank the Senior Minister of State.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: The Senior Minister of State mentioned that there will be cost support.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: But is there a reason why insurance is not offered, rather than general cost support?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Two, I thank the Senior Minister of State for saying there will be flexibility for IT-incapable practices, such as the senior GPs who are my constituents.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Can the Senior Minister of State just double click and explain a bit what this flexibility for IT-incapable practices might entail?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Three, I think I did not hear an answer to what if there is a data breach.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: Can the insurers now use the now-public information in the data breach?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: And I thank him for his response to my concerns about the inspection and right to audit clauses.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: The Senior Minister of State's response is that doctors should carefully assess what is relevant.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: I think that this may not be a great solution because I think the doctor is caught in the middle between the insurer and the patient, and they have to bear liability for the judgement calls as to what they put in the notes.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: So, I think what is probably going to happen is that there is going to be a chilling effect, where doctors will start avoiding documenting any sensitive data, both in their own medical records but also perhaps in NEHR as well.

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: And so, if it percolates up to the NEHR, would the NEHR utility not be undermined if they cannot trust what to input?

speaker: Mr Kenneth Tiong Boon Kiat
text: So, I mentioned in my speech that it might be better to just go downstream and just say that we "work with MAS to prohibit insurers from requiring NEHR-derived information as a condition of coverage, claim processing and policy renewal." And if I may, that is a significant part of why I posed the Parliamentary Question to Minister Ong Ye Kung earlier today about needing a dual regulation framework by MAS and MOH for insurers, so that someone is cleanly accountable for insurer behaviour as a health system actor.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: I believe there are four clarifications and I will take them in turn.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: One about offering cyber insurance to GP clinics.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: Can I just get the Member to confirm that this is what he is asking about?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And there are a number of support packages we are discussing with them.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: These details we will make known in due course.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: We are supporting them, and we want them to travel the journey together with us.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And there is broad support among the doctors, including those smaller GPs who see the value of contributing to and assessing NEHR, and most of the GPs are already onboard.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: They understand the need for the cybersecurity and data security requirements under the Bill to protect the data, and we are working with them to look at the various whitelisted services and management systems they can adopt to meet the requirements.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: So, if this is something useful, we will certainly consider as part of the support packages and discussions with the relevant stakeholders.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: If the Member could clarify on third question for me, please?

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But in data breaches, I think it all boils down to the ethical considerations or how they access those data breaches in the first place, and that is something we have to work together with MAS, as the regulator, together with insurance companies, on understanding how they are using that information.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And that is something we frown upon – using NEHR data for purpose of insurance.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But it is a hypothetical scenario, something we have to think through.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: On a dedicated regulation around insurance, whether they should just be prohibited, to avoid putting the healthcare providers or professionals in a very difficult situation – this is something we are working through with the healthcare providers, the industry associations as well as together with MAS with the insurance industry.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: In fact, I had mentioned earlier in my closing speech that MOH has issued guidelines to the insurers and doctors on how we should think about the HIB when it is enacted.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: And we have to work through the insurance associations, the MAS, the professional bodies, including the healthcare professional bodies for how it is implemented on the ground.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But our assurance to the public and to those Members who spoke about it, is that our approach and position is quite clear.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: I wonder if I heard clearly that the access to information to electronic medical records by healthcare professionals will be captured in the NEHR access history.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: I ask this because the Singaporean who was particularly concerned about this Bill sent me the URL to the FAQ in HealthHub that reads, "Your healthcare professionals may be accessing your records from their own electronic medical records (EMR) systems.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: Access made to your records in their EMR systems are not included in the NEHR access history." I would be happy to share the URL.

speaker: Mr David Hoe
text: I just wanted to clarify whether what I heard was correct.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: It is an internal operations system for the hospitals, for the polyclinics or for the private healthcare clinics.

speaker: Mr Tan Kiat How
text: But if you use EMR to log to NEHR, the logs will be recorded and tracked.

speaker: Mr Speaker
text: Any other clarifications from Members for the Senior Minister of State?
